chapters.summary_md: Women of the city blamed the wife of the Aziz; she gathered them, they were amazed at Yusuf, and she threatened him with prison; Yusuf asked God to turn their plotting away from him, and God answered him [c1][c2][c3][c4][c5].
chapters.body_md:
Women in the city said that the wife of the Aziz was seducing her young manservant, that love for him had gripped her, and that they saw her in clear error [c1]. When she heard of their scheming, she sent for them and prepared a place for them to recline, and gave each of them a knife; then she told Yusuf to come out before them [c2]. When they saw him they were amazed at him and cut their hands, and they said, glorifying God, that this was no human being but a noble angel [c2]. She told them that this was the one they had blamed her for, that she had tried to seduce him and he had held back, and that if he did not do what she ordered him, he would be imprisoned and be among the humiliated [c3].

Yusuf said to his Lord that prison was dearer to him than what they called him to, and that unless God turned their plotting away from him he might incline to them and be among the ignorant [c4]. His Lord answered him and turned their plotting away from him; He hears and knows [c5].
chapters.deep_md: The scene turns on the women's remark (12:30) [c1] and the gathering she arranged in reply (12:31) [c2]. Yusuf's words in 12:33 prefer prison to what he is called to and ask God for protection [c4]; 12:34 gives the answer [c5].
chapters.kids_md: Some women in the city blamed the wife of the Aziz [c1]. She invited them and gave each a knife, then told Yusuf to come out; they were so amazed that they cut their hands [c2]. Yusuf asked God to keep their plotting away from him, and God answered his prayer [c4][c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): In this scene Yusuf's words are a prayer: he prefers prison to wrongdoing and asks God to turn the plotting away from him [c4]. One reading is that the passage holds up asking God for protection when one fears one's own weakness [c4]. The text says God answered him [c5].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not say who the women were or how many, or what the knives were for beyond giving each one a knife. It says they cut their hands and gives no further detail.
- It does not describe Yusuf, or what the women saw; the verses record only their amazement and their words.
- It does not say how long after the previous events this was.
- 'Aziz' is a title; the Quran does not say what office it names. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: later accounts give the Aziz and his wife personal names; none is used here.

claims.statement_en: After they had seen the signs, it occurred to them to imprison Yusuf for a time.

Two young men entered the prison with him; one said he saw himself pressing wine, and the other that he saw himself carrying bread on his head, from which birds were eating; they asked Yusuf to tell them the interpretation, for they saw him as one of those who do good.

Yusuf said that no food provided for them would come before he had informed them of its interpretation; this, he said, was from what his Lord had taught him; and he had left the way of a people who do not believe in God and who deny the Hereafter.

He said that he followed the way of his forefathers Ibrahim, Ishaq and Yaqub, that it was not for them to associate anything with God, and that this was from God's favour on them and on people, though most people are not thankful.

Speaking to his companions in prison, Yusuf asked whether scattered lords were better, or God, who is one and prevails over all; he said that what they worshipped besides Him were only names that they and their fathers had given, for which God had sent down no authority; that judgement belongs to God alone, who had commanded them to worship none but Him; and that this is the right religion, though most people do not know.
Yusuf gave the interpretation: one of them would serve wine to his lord, and the other would be crucified and the birds would eat from his head; the matter about which they asked was decided.

Yusuf said to the one he thought would be saved that he should mention him to his lord; Satan caused a forgetting of the mention of his lord (the Arabic can be read as the freed man forgetting to mention Yusuf to his master, or as Yusuf forgetting to mention his own Lord), and Yusuf remained in prison for several years.

chapters.summary_md: Yusuf was imprisoned; two young men there told him dreams, and he called them to worship God alone and gave the interpretations: one would serve wine, the other would be crucified [c1][c2][c5][c6]. He asked the one who would be saved to mention him, and stayed in prison for several years [c7].
chapters.body_md:
After they had seen the signs, it occurred to them to imprison Yusuf for a time [c1]. Two young men entered the prison with him [c2]. One said he saw himself pressing wine; the other that he saw himself carrying bread on his head, from which birds were eating [c2]. They asked Yusuf to tell them the interpretation, for they saw him as one of those who do good [c2].

Yusuf told them that no food provided for them would come before he had informed them of its interpretation; this, he said, was from what his Lord had taught him, and he had left the way of a people who do not believe in God and who deny the Hereafter [c3]. He said he followed the way of his forefathers Ibrahim, Ishaq and Yaqub, that it was not for them to associate anything with God, and that this was from God's favour on them and on people, though most people are not thankful [c4]. Speaking to his companions in prison, he asked whether scattered lords were better, or God, who is one and prevails over all; he said that what they worshipped besides Him were only names that they and their fathers had given, for which God had sent down no authority; that judgement belongs to God alone, who had commanded them to worship none but Him; and that this is the right religion, though most people do not know [c5].

Then he gave the interpretation: one of them would serve wine to his lord, and the other would be crucified and the birds would eat from his head; the matter about which they asked was decided [c6]. He said to the one he thought would be saved that he should mention him to his lord [c7]. Satan caused a forgetting of the mention of his lord (the Arabic can be read as the freed man forgetting to mention Yusuf to his master, or as Yusuf forgetting to mention his own Lord), and Yusuf remained in prison for several years [c7].
chapters.deep_md: Yusuf prefaces the interpretation with what his Lord taught him and the way he follows (12:37-38) [c3][c4], then a call to worship God alone (12:39-40) [c5], and only then gives the interpretation (12:41) [c6]. The request itself is in 12:36 [c2].
chapters.kids_md: Two young men came into the prison with Yusuf and told him their dreams [c2]. Yusuf told them first that he followed the way of Ibrahim, Ishaq and Yaqub and worshipped God alone [c4][c5]. Then he told them what their dreams meant [c6]. He asked the one who would be freed to mention him, but Yusuf stayed in prison for several years [c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): Yusuf is asked for help with a dream and first speaks about worship of God alone [c2][c5]. One reading is that he treats the request as a chance to state his belief, and then gives the interpretation [c3][c5][c6]. The passage also records that he stayed in prison for several years after asking [c7].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not name the two young men or say what they had done; it does not say who 'his lord' in 12:41 is.
- It does not say how long 'a time' (12:35) was, how old Yusuf was when he was imprisoned, what the signs were that they had seen, or who 'they' are who decided on the prison.
- The Arabic for 'several years' does not give an exact number of years.
- The reference of 'his lord' in 12:42 can be read in two ways, as noted in the text; the verse does not settle it.

claims.statement_en: The king said that he saw seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain and other dry ones; he asked his chiefs to explain his vision if they could interpret visions.
They said that it was a confusion of dreams and that they had no knowledge of the interpretation of such dreams.

The one who had been saved remembered after a period, said that he would inform them of its interpretation and asked to be sent; he came to Yusuf, addressed him as the truthful one, and asked for the interpretation of the cows and the ears, so that he might return to the people and they might know.
Yusuf said that they would sow for seven years continuously, and that what they harvested they should leave in its ear, except a little for eating.
Yusuf said that after that would come seven hard years that would eat what they had stored for them, except a little of what they preserved.
Yusuf said that after that would come a year in which people would be given relief and in which they would press.

chapters.summary_md: The king dreamed of seven fat cows eaten by seven lean ones, and of seven green ears and dry ones; the man who had been saved from prison came to Yusuf, who gave the interpretation: seven years of sowing, seven hard years, then a year of relief [c1][c3][c4][c5][c6].
chapters.body_md:
The king said that he saw seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain and other dry ones; he asked his chiefs to explain his vision if they could interpret visions [c1]. They said it was a confusion of dreams and that they had no knowledge of the interpretation of such dreams [c2]. The one who had been saved remembered after a period, said that he would inform them of its interpretation, and asked to be sent; he came to Yusuf, addressed him as the truthful one, and asked for the interpretation of the cows and the ears, so that he might return to the people and they might know [c3].

Yusuf said that they would sow for seven years continuously, and that what they harvested they should leave in its ear, except a little for eating [c4]. After that, he said, would come seven hard years that would eat what they had stored for them, except a little of what they preserved [c5]. After that would come a year in which people would be given relief and in which they would press [c6].
chapters.deep_md: The king's dream has a part about cows and a part about ears [c1]. Yusuf's interpretation follows the dream in order: seven years of growing (12:47) [c4], seven hard years (12:48) [c5], then a year of relief (12:49) [c6]. In it Yusuf also gives instructions: leave the harvest in its ear except a little to eat [c4], and preserve a little [c5].
chapters.kids_md: The king dreamed of seven fat cows eaten by seven thin ones, and seven green ears of grain with dry ones [c1]. His chiefs could not explain it [c2]. The man who had left prison remembered Yusuf and asked him [c3]. Yusuf said there would be seven years of growing, then seven hard years, then a year of relief [c4][c5][c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): Yusuf's interpretation includes what to do in the good years: leave the harvest in its ear and keep only a little to eat [c4][c5]. One reading is that preparing in good times for hard times is presented as part of the interpretation [c4][c5].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not name the king or the land he ruled. It uses the word king for the ruler in this account. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: later accounts name the king and give him a dynasty and a title; none is used here.
- It does not say who the chiefs were or how long the 'period' of 12:45 was.
- The Arabic for 'press' does not say what was pressed (grapes, olives or something else).
- It does not say how the king knew to ask for an interpretation, or how long after the prison scene this came.

claims.statement_en: The king ordered that Yusuf be brought to him; when the messenger came, Yusuf told him to return to his lord and ask him about the women who had cut their hands, for Yusuf's Lord knows their plotting.

The king asked the women what their affair was when they tried to seduce Yusuf; they said that, God forbid, they knew no evil against him; and the wife of the Aziz said that now the truth had become clear: she was the one who had tried to seduce him, and he was among the truthful.

A speech follows, in which the speaker says that this was so that the master would know that he had not betrayed him in his absence, and that God does not guide the plotting of the betrayers; and that he does not declare himself innocent, for the self commands evil except where his Lord has mercy, and his Lord is forgiving and merciful.
The king said to bring Yusuf to him, that he would take him for himself; and when he had spoken with him, he told Yusuf that he was that day established with them and trusted.
Yusuf asked to be set over the storehouses of the land, saying that he was a knowing guardian.
God says that in this way He established Yusuf in the land, where he could settle wherever he wished; He reaches with His mercy whomever He wills and does not waste the reward of those who do good.
The reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and are mindful of God.

chapters.summary_md: The king sent for Yusuf; Yusuf asked first about the women who had cut their hands; the wife of the Aziz admitted she had tried to seduce him; the king found him trusted, Yusuf asked to be set over the storehouses of the land, and God says He established him in the land [c1][c2][c4][c5][c6].
chapters.body_md:
The king ordered that Yusuf be brought to him [c1]. When the messenger came, Yusuf told him to return to his lord and ask him about the women who had cut their hands, for Yusuf's Lord knows their plotting [c1]. The king asked the women what their affair was when they tried to seduce Yusuf; they said that, God forbid, they knew no evil against him; and the wife of the Aziz said that now the truth had become clear: she was the one who had tried to seduce him, and he was among the truthful [c2].

A speech follows, read here as Yusuf's: this was so that the master would know that he had not betrayed him in his absence, and that God does not guide the plotting of the betrayers; and he does not declare himself innocent, for the self commands evil except where his Lord has mercy, and his Lord is forgiving and merciful [c3].

The king said to bring Yusuf to him, that he would take him for himself; and when he had spoken with him, he told Yusuf that he was that day established with them and trusted [c4]. Yusuf asked to be set over the storehouses of the land, saying that he was a knowing guardian [c5]. God says that in this way He established Yusuf in the land, where he could settle wherever he wished; He reaches with His mercy whomever He wills and does not waste the reward of those who do good [c6]. The reward of the Hereafter, the Quran adds, is better for those who believe and are mindful of God [c7].
chapters.deep_md: The central scene is the king's questioning of the women (12:51) [c2]. Yusuf's request in 12:50 comes before it [c1], and the speech in 12:52-53 after it [c3]. The passage ends with Yusuf's request for a post (12:55) [c5] and God's statement about establishing him (12:56) [c6].
chapters.kids_md: The king asked for Yusuf to be brought out, and Yusuf asked him to find out the truth about the women first [c1]. The wife of the Aziz said that she had been the one at fault and that Yusuf was truthful [c2]. The king trusted Yusuf, and Yusuf asked to look after the storehouses of the land [c4][c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): Yusuf asks that the truth of the matter be examined before he comes out [c1], and the truth is stated aloud [c2]. One reading is that the passage values clearing a matter openly [c1][c2]. In the speech that follows, the speaker does not declare himself innocent and says that the self commands evil unless God has mercy [c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not say how long after the dream these events came, or give the title or rank of the post Yusuf asked for; it says 'the storehouses of the land'.
- The verses do not say who speaks 12:52-53. This draft reads them as Yusuf's; a reviewer must confirm, because the verses do not name the speaker.
- The Quran does not narrate the moment of Yusuf's release; he says later (12:100) that God brought him out of the prison.
- It does not say in so many words that the king granted the post; 12:56 says God established Yusuf in the land.

claims.statement_en: Yusuf's brothers came and entered where he was; he recognised them, but they did not recognise him.

When Yusuf had supplied them with their provisions, he told them to bring him a brother of theirs from their father, and asked whether they did not see that he gave full measure and was the best of hosts.
He said that if they did not bring him, there would be no measure for them from him and they should not come near him.
They said that they would try to persuade his father about him and would do so.
Yusuf told his servants to put the brothers' goods back in their saddlebags, so that they would recognise them when they returned to their family and might come back.

When they went back to their father they said that the measure had been withheld from them, and asked him to send their brother with them so that they could have their measure, promising to guard him.
Their father asked whether he should entrust him to them as he had entrusted them with his brother before, and said that God is the best guardian and the most merciful of the merciful.

When they opened their goods and found their merchandise returned, they said that they wanted nothing more: they would bring supplies for their family, guard their brother, and add a camel's load, which was an easy measure.

Their father said that he would not send him with them until they gave him a pledge by God that they would bring him back unless they were surrounded; when they gave their pledge, he said that God was guardian over what they said.

He told them not to enter by one gate but by different gates, though he could avail them nothing against God, for judgement belongs to God alone and in Him he put his trust; and when they entered as their father had ordered, it availed them nothing against God, but it met a need in Yaqub's soul which he fulfilled; he had knowledge because God had taught him, though most people do not know.

chapters.summary_md: Yusuf's brothers came to him for supplies; he recognised them and they did not recognise him; he asked them to bring their other brother, and their father agreed only after a pledge by God [c1][c2][c3][c9].
chapters.body_md:
Yusuf's brothers came and entered where he was; he recognised them, but they did not recognise him [c1]. When he had supplied them with their provisions, he told them to bring him a brother of theirs from their father, and asked whether they did not see that he gave full measure and was the best of hosts [c2]. If they did not bring him, he said, there would be no measure for them from him and they should not come near him [c3]. They said they would try to persuade his father about him [c4]. Yusuf told his servants to put the brothers' goods back in their saddlebags, so that they would recognise them when they returned to their family and might come back [c5].

When they went back to their father, they said that the measure had been withheld from them, and asked him to send their brother with them so that they could have their measure, promising to guard him [c6]. Their father asked whether he should entrust him to them as he had entrusted them with his brother before; God, he said, is the best guardian and the most merciful of the merciful [c7]. When they opened their goods and found their merchandise returned, they said they wanted nothing more: they would bring supplies for their family, guard their brother, and add a camel's load, which was an easy measure [c8]. Their father said he would not send him with them until they gave him a pledge by God that they would bring him back unless they were surrounded; when they gave their pledge, he said that God was guardian over what they said [c9].

He told them not to enter by one gate but by different gates, though he could avail them nothing against God, for judgement belongs to God alone and in Him he put his trust [c10]. When they entered as their father had ordered, it availed them nothing against God, but it met a need in Yaqub's soul which he fulfilled; he had knowledge because God had taught him, though most people do not know [c10].
chapters.deep_md: The passage shows Yusuf's request (12:59-60) [c2][c3], the brothers' agreement (12:61) [c4], the return of their goods (12:62) [c5], and the father's conditions (12:64-68) [c7][c9][c10].
chapters.kids_md: Yusuf's brothers came to him for food [c1]. He knew them, but they did not know him [c1]. He asked them to bring their other brother [c2]. Their father said he would send him only if they promised before God to bring him back [c9].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): Their father ties his agreement to a pledge by God and also gives practical advice, to enter by different gates, while saying that judgement belongs to God alone [c9][c10]. One reading is that taking precautions and trusting God are presented together in this passage [c10].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not say how Yusuf knew of the brother or why he asked for him.
- It does not say when the brothers came, how many years it had been since they parted from Yusuf, or how many came.
- It gives no reason why the brothers did not recognise Yusuf; it says only that they did not.
- It does not say why the father told them to enter by different gates, or what the need in Yaqub's soul was.
- It does not name the brother. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: later accounts name Yusuf's full brother; the name is not used here.

chapters.title_en: The brother and the king's cup

claims.statement_en: When the brothers came in to Yusuf, he took his brother aside and told him that he was his brother, so he should not grieve over what the others had been doing.
When Yusuf had supplied them with provisions, he placed the drinking cup in his brother's saddlebag, and then a caller cried out that the caravan were thieves.

The brothers turned and asked what they were missing; they were told that the king's measuring cup was missing, that whoever brought it would have a camel's load, and that the speaker was responsible for it.
The brothers said, by God, that they knew they had not come to cause corruption in the land and were not thieves.

They asked what the penalty would be if they were found to be liars; the answer was that the penalty would be the one in whose saddlebag it was found, who himself would be the penalty, for that is how they penalise wrongdoers.

Yusuf began with their bags before his brother's bag, and then brought the cup out of his brother's bag; God says that in this way He devised for Yusuf; he could not have taken his brother under the king's law unless God willed; God raises in degrees whom He wills, and above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows more.

The brothers said that if he had stolen, a brother of his had stolen before; Yusuf kept this in himself and did not reveal it to them, and said that they were in a worse position and that God knew best what they described.

They addressed Yusuf as the Aziz and said that the boy had a very old father, and asked him to take one of them in his place, since they saw him as one of those who do good; he said that God forbid that they should take anyone but the one in whose possession they had found their property, for then they would be wrongdoers.

When they despaired of him, they withdrew to confer privately; the eldest of them reminded the rest that their father had taken a pledge from them before God and that they had failed regarding Yusuf before; he said that he would not leave the land until his father permitted him or God judged for him, for God is the best of judges.

The eldest told them to return to their father and say that his son had stolen, that they testified only to what they knew and had not been guardians of the unseen, and that he could ask the town where they had been and the caravan with which they came, for they were truthful.

chapters.summary_md: Yusuf told his brother privately that he was his brother, then the king's cup was placed in his brother's bag and found there; Yusuf kept his brother and refused the others' plea to take another in his place [c1][c2][c6][c8].
chapters.body_md:
When the brothers came in to Yusuf, he took his brother aside and told him that he was his brother, so he should not grieve over what the others had been doing [c1]. When he had supplied them with provisions, he placed the drinking cup in his brother's saddlebag, and then a caller cried out that the caravan were thieves [c2]. The brothers turned and asked what they were missing; they were told that the king's measuring cup was missing, that whoever brought it would have a camel's load, and that the speaker was responsible for it [c3]. The brothers said, by God, that they knew they had not come to cause corruption in the land and were not thieves [c4]. They asked what the penalty would be if they were found to be liars; the answer was that the penalty would be the one in whose saddlebag it was found, who himself would be the penalty, for that is how they penalise wrongdoers [c5].

Yusuf began with their bags before his brother's bag, and then brought the cup out of his brother's bag [c6]. God says that in this way He devised for Yusuf; he could not have taken his brother under the king's law unless God willed; God raises in degrees whom He wills, and above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows more [c6]. The brothers said that if he had stolen, a brother of his had stolen before; Yusuf kept this in himself and did not reveal it to them, and said that they were in a worse position and that God knew best what they described [c7]. They addressed Yusuf as the Aziz and said that the boy had a very old father, and asked him to take one of them in his place, since they saw him as one of those who do good; he said that God forbid that they should take anyone but the one in whose possession they had found their property, for then they would be wrongdoers [c8].

When they despaired of him, they withdrew to confer privately [c9]. The eldest of them reminded the rest that their father had taken a pledge from them before God and that they had failed regarding Yusuf before; he said that he would not leave the land until his father permitted him or God judged for him, for God is the best of judges [c9]. He told them to return to their father and say that his son had stolen, that they testified only to what they knew and had not been guardians of the unseen, and that he could ask the town where they had been and the caravan with which they came, for they were truthful [c10].
chapters.deep_md: The scene is told in a sequence of statements: the private word to the brother (12:69) [c1], the cup and the cry (12:70-72) [c2][c3], the protest and the agreed penalty (12:73-75) [c4][c5], the search (12:76) [c6], the remark about an earlier theft (12:77) [c7], the plea and the refusal (12:78-79) [c8], and the decision of the eldest (12:80-82) [c9][c10]. The verse 12:76 states that the device was God's, and that Yusuf could not have kept his brother under the king's law unless God willed [c6].
chapters.kids_md: Yusuf told his brother quietly that he was his brother [c1]. The king's cup was found in his brother's bag, and Yusuf kept him there [c2][c6]. The other brothers asked Yusuf to take one of them instead, but Yusuf said no [c8]. The eldest brother decided to stay in the land until his father allowed him to leave or God judged for him [c9].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The eldest brother's words recall the pledge to their father and the earlier failure over Yusuf [c9]. One reading is that the brothers, facing a similar loss, now plead to protect the one who remains [c8][c9].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not say who the caller was, or whether Yusuf's brother knew of the plan beforehand; it says only that Yusuf told him who he was.
- It does not describe the cup (it uses different words for it), or say what material it was.
- It does not say what the earlier theft by 'a brother of his' (12:77) was. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: later accounts tell a story to explain this remark; none is used here.
- It does not say which brother is 'the eldest' or how the decision was reached.
- How the 'king's law' of 12:76 worked is not described.
- How Yusuf's placing of the cup (12:70-76) is to be assessed is not discussed in the verses beyond saying that it was God's device; this draft gives no verdict on it and leaves the matter to the scholarly reviewer.

claims.statement_en: The father said that rather their souls had enticed them to something, that his course was graceful patience, and that perhaps God would bring them all to him; God, he said, is the knowing, the wise.
He turned away from them and said how great was his sorrow over Yusuf; his eyes turned white from grief, and he was suppressing it.
His sons said that, by God, he would not cease remembering Yusuf until he was ruined or among the perishing.
He answered that he complained of his distress and sorrow only to God, and that he knew from God what they did not know.
He told his sons to go and inquire about Yusuf and his brother, and not to despair of God's mercy, for none despairs of God's mercy except the disbelieving people.

chapters.summary_md: On hearing the brothers' report, their father said again that his course was graceful patience; he grieved over Yusuf, complained only to God, and told his sons to search for Yusuf and his brother and not to despair of God's mercy [c1][c2][c4][c5].
chapters.body_md: The father said to his sons that rather their souls had enticed them to something, that his course was graceful patience, and that perhaps God would bring them all to him; God, he said, is the knowing, the wise [c1]. He turned away from them and said how great was his sorrow over Yusuf; his eyes turned white from grief, and he was suppressing it [c2]. His sons said that, by God, he would not cease remembering Yusuf until he was ruined or among the perishing [c3]. He answered that he complained of his distress and sorrow only to God, and that he knew from God what they did not know [c4]. He told them to go and inquire about Yusuf and his brother, and not to despair of God's mercy, for none despairs of God's mercy except the disbelieving people [c5].
chapters.deep_md: The passage joins the father's grief (12:84) [c2], the sons' reproach (12:85) [c3], his reply that he complains only to God (12:86) [c4], and his instruction not to despair of God's mercy (12:87) [c5].
chapters.kids_md: Their father said he would be patient, and that God might bring them all back to him [c1]. He was very sad about Yusuf, and he told God about his sadness [c2][c4]. He told his sons to go and look for Yusuf and his brother, and never to give up hope in God's mercy [c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The father's grief is stated plainly, and so is where he takes it: he complains only to God and tells his sons not to despair of God's mercy [c2][c4][c5]. One reading is that the passage joins honest sorrow with continued hope [c2][c5].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not say how long it had been since Yusuf was lost.
- The verse says his eyes turned white from grief; it does not say whether he lost his sight (a later verse, 12:96, speaks of his returning seeing).
- It does not say what the father knew from God (12:86).
- The father's first sentence repeats the words he used at 12:18.
- The father is not named in these verses; he is named elsewhere in the surah (12:6, 12:38, 12:68).

claims.statement_en: The brothers entered on Yusuf and addressed him as the Aziz, saying that hardship had touched them and their family; they had brought poor merchandise, and asked him to give them full measure and to be charitable to them, for God rewards the charitable.
Yusuf asked whether they knew what they had done with Yusuf and his brother when they were ignorant.

They asked whether he was indeed Yusuf, and he said that he was Yusuf and that this was his brother, that God had been gracious to them, and that whoever is mindful of God and patient finds that God does not waste the reward of those who do good.
They said, by God, that God had preferred him over them, and that they had been sinners.
Yusuf said that there was no blame on them that day, that God forgives them, and that He is the most merciful of the merciful.
Yusuf told them to take his shirt and throw it over his father's face, and he would come seeing; and to bring all their family to him.

chapters.summary_md: The brothers came back in need; Yusuf asked whether they knew what they had done with Yusuf and his brother, and told them who he was; they admitted their wrong, he said there was no blame on them that day, and he sent his shirt to his father [c2][c3][c4][c5][c6].
chapters.body_md: The brothers entered on Yusuf and addressed him as the Aziz, saying that hardship had touched them and their family; they had brought poor merchandise, and they asked him to give them full measure and to be charitable to them, for God rewards the charitable [c1]. He asked whether they knew what they had done with Yusuf and his brother when they were ignorant [c2]. They asked whether he was indeed Yusuf, and he said that he was Yusuf and that this was his brother, that God had been gracious to them, and that whoever is mindful of God and patient finds that God does not waste the reward of those who do good [c3]. They said, by God, that God had preferred him over them, and that they had been sinners [c4]. He said there was no blame on them that day, that God forgives them, and that He is the most merciful of the merciful [c5]. He told them to take his shirt and throw it over his father's face, and he would come seeing; and to bring all their family to him [c6].
chapters.deep_md: Yusuf's making himself known moves in short steps: the plea (12:88) [c1], his question (12:89) [c2], their question and his answer (12:90) [c3], their acknowledgement (12:91) [c4], and his words of release (12:92) [c5]. The instruction about the shirt in 12:93 sends the news to the father [c6].
chapters.kids_md: The brothers came back needing help [c1]. Yusuf asked if they knew what they had done to Yusuf and his brother [c2]. They asked if he was Yusuf, and he said he was, and that this was his brother [c3]. They said they had been wrong [c4]. Yusuf said there was no blame on them that day and that God forgives them [c5]. He sent his shirt for his father [c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): Yusuf answers their admission with the words that there is no blame on them that day and that God forgives them [c4][c5]. One reading is that the text places forgiveness at the moment when the wrong is acknowledged [c4][c5]. He also names patience and mindfulness of God as the way in which God does not waste the reward of those who do good [c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not say what led them to ask whether he was Yusuf.
- It does not say how many years had passed since the first visit, or where the meeting took place beyond 'before him'.
- It does not say whether the shirt is the same shirt as in the earlier scenes, or that it had any property beyond Yusuf's instruction.

claims.statement_en: When the caravan set out, their father said that he found the scent of Yusuf, unless they thought him weak-minded.
Others said that, by God, he was in his old error.
When the bearer of good news came, he cast the shirt on the father's face, and the father returned seeing; he said, did he not tell them that he knew from God what they did not know.
His sons asked their father to ask forgiveness for their sins, since they had been sinners, and he said he would ask forgiveness for them from his Lord, who is forgiving and merciful.
When they entered on Yusuf, he took his parents to himself and told them to enter Egypt, if God willed, in safety.

Yusuf raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration; he said that this was the interpretation of his dream of before, which his Lord had made true; that his Lord had been good to him in bringing him out of the prison and in bringing them from the desert, after Satan had stirred up enmity between him and his brothers; and that his Lord is subtle in what He wills, the knowing, the wise.

Yusuf prayed that God, who had given him of the kingdom and taught him the interpretation of events, and who is the creator of the heavens and the earth, would take him as one who submits and join him with the righteous.

chapters.summary_md: As the caravan set out, the father said he found the scent of Yusuf; when the shirt was cast on his face he returned seeing; the sons asked his forgiveness; the family came to Yusuf, who said his dream of before had come true and prayed to be taken as one who submits and joined with the righteous [c1][c3][c4][c5][c6][c7].
chapters.body_md:
When the caravan set out, their father said that he found the scent of Yusuf, unless they thought him weak-minded [c1]. Others said that, by God, he was in his old error [c2]. When the bearer of good news came, he cast the shirt on the father's face, and the father returned seeing; he said, did he not tell them that he knew from God what they did not know [c3]. His sons asked their father to ask forgiveness for their sins, since they had been sinners, and he said he would ask forgiveness for them from his Lord, who is forgiving and merciful [c4].

When they entered on Yusuf, he took his parents to himself and told them to enter Egypt, if God willed, in safety [c5]. He raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration [c6]. Yusuf said that this was the interpretation of his dream of before, which his Lord had made true; that his Lord had been good to him in bringing him out of the prison and in bringing them from the desert, after Satan had stirred up enmity between him and his brothers; and that his Lord is subtle in what He wills, the knowing, the wise [c6]. He prayed that God, who had given him of the kingdom and taught him the interpretation of events, and who is the creator of the heavens and the earth, would take him as one who submits and join him with the righteous [c7].
chapters.deep_md: The passage runs from the sign of the shirt (12:94-96) [c1][c3] to the father's promise (12:97-98) [c4], the family's arrival (12:99-100) [c5][c6] and Yusuf's prayer (12:101) [c7]. At 12:100 Yusuf calls the scene the interpretation of his dream of before [c6].
chapters.kids_md: When the caravan set out, Yusuf's father said he found the scent of Yusuf [c1]. The shirt was put on his face, and he returned seeing [c3]. The brothers asked him to ask for forgiveness for them, and he said he would [c4]. When the family came to Yusuf, he took his parents to himself [c5]. Yusuf said that his dream of before had come true [c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The brothers ask for forgiveness and the father promises to ask it from his Lord [c4]. Yusuf calls the reunion the interpretation of his earlier dream and credits it to his Lord [c6]. One reading is that the passage ends not with triumph but with a prayer to be taken as one who submits [c7].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not say how much time passed between the first dream and the reunion; Yusuf calls the dream one 'of before'.
- It does not say who 'others' are in 12:95.
- It does not say how many people were in the family. Later accounts differ on who 'his parents' (12:99-100) were; the verses do not say.
- The father is not named in these verses; he is named elsewhere in the surah (12:6, 12:38, 12:68).
- It does not say what the prostration in 12:100 was, whether greeting, honour or something else.
- The Arabic verb in Yusuf's prayer (12:101) is the one used for taking a soul; how to render it is left to the reviewer.
- It does not narrate what became of the brothers, or Yusuf's death.

claims.statement_en: Yusuf had come to those addressed before with clear proofs, but they stayed in doubt about what he brought until he died; then they said that God would never send a messenger after him; in this way, the verse says, God leaves in error whoever is a transgressor and a doubter.

chapters.summary_md: Another surah recalls that Yusuf came with clear proofs, that those addressed doubted what he brought until he died, and that they then said God would send no messenger after him [c1].
chapters.body_md: A verse in another surah speaks of Yusuf: he had come to those addressed with clear proofs before, but they stayed in doubt about what he brought, until he died; then they said that God would never send a messenger after him [c1]. The verse adds that in this way God leaves in error whoever is a transgressor and a doubter [c1].
chapters.deep_md: The verse does not retell the story; it recalls one fact about Yusuf's mission, that he came with clear proofs, and one reaction after his death [c1].
chapters.kids_md: Another surah says that Yusuf came with clear proofs, but the people kept doubting [c1].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): The verse shows a people doubting what a messenger brought and then, after his death, speaking as if no messenger would follow [c1]. One reading is that the verse invites reflection on doubt that persists in the face of clear proofs [c1].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- The Quran does not say who those addressed are, or when this was; the verse belongs to a passage (around 40:28-35) outside this draft's range.
- It does not say what the clear proofs were.
- It does not say to whom Yusuf came in the sense of this verse, or where.

uncertainties_en: Hadith to add later: authenticated narrations, each with a named grader, about Yusuf. None is used in this draft.

The verses 12:1-3 (the framing of the surah) and 12:102-111 (the closing passage) are outside the inventory range for Yusuf and are not used. A reviewer should decide whether to extend the inventory and add framing and closing chapters.
12:24 (the verse about what she and he were set on): the Arabic about his part is read in more than one way; the draft states only the verse's condition and a reviewer must check the wording.
The speaker of 12:52-53 is not named in the verses; the draft reads it as Yusuf's and marks it so.
The reference of 'his lord' in 12:42 is open (the released man's master or Yusuf's own Lord); the draft keeps both readings.
The 'lord' of 12:23 can mean his master or his Lord; the draft keeps both.
How Yusuf's placing of the cup (12:70-76) is to be assessed is not given in the verses beyond calling it God's device; the draft gives no verdict and a scholar should look at it.
Who the 'parents' of 12:99-100 are is not stated; the draft does not decide.

Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: personal names for Yusuf's brothers, mother, the Aziz, his wife and the king; the name and the story of the wolf; where the well was; many details of the prison scenes. None is used in the story texts.
The only numbers used are those stated by the verses: eleven stars (12:4), seven cows and ears and years (12:43-49), several years in prison (12:42). No age, year or duration is given beyond these.
Arabic and Urdu texts are not written; they are left null for translators.

claims.statement_en: God recites the news of Musa and Fir'awn in truth, for a people who believe.
Fir'awn exalted himself in the land, made its people into factions, oppressed one group of them, slaughtering their sons and keeping their women alive; he was among the corrupters.
God says He wished to favour those who were oppressed in the land, make them leaders and inheritors, establish them in the land, and show Fir'awn, Haman and their soldiers what they feared from them.
God inspired the mother of Musa and told her “Nurse him; and when you fear for him, cast him into the river and do not fear or grieve; we will return him to you and make him one of the messengers.”

In another passage, God reminds Musa that He had favoured him another time, when He inspired his mother what was inspired: to put him in the chest and put it into the river, so that the river would cast it up on the bank where an enemy of God and of Musa would take him.
God says He cast love from Himself upon Musa, so that he would be brought up under His eye.

chapters.summary_md: The account begins with Fir'awn's oppression of one group in his land [c2] and God's wish to favour the oppressed [c3]. God inspired the mother of Musa to nurse him and, when she feared, to cast him into the river, with a promise to return him and make him a messenger [c4]. Another passage tells the same favour with the chest [c5].
chapters.body_md:
God says He recites the news of Musa and Fir'awn in truth for a people who believe [c1]. Fir'awn exalted himself in the land and divided its people into factions, oppressing one group by slaughtering their sons and keeping their women alive [c2]. God says He wished to favour the oppressed, make them leaders and inheritors, and show Fir'awn, Haman and their soldiers what they feared [c3].

God inspired Musa's mother: nurse him, and when you fear for him, cast him into the river; do not fear or grieve; He would return him to her and make him one of the messengers [c4]. Another passage recalls this as a further favour: the child was to be put in a chest and the chest in the river, which would cast it on the bank, where an enemy of God and of Musa would take him [c5]. God cast love from Himself upon Musa so that he would be brought up under His eye [c6].
chapters.deep_md: One passage frames the decree with Fir'awn's policy and God's wish to favour the oppressed [c2][c3], then gives the instruction to the mother with a promise [c4]. Another gives the instruction as a favour recalled to Musa himself and adds the chest and the bank [c5], and the love cast upon him [c6]. Both agree on the river [c4][c5]. Haman is already named as one of the people God wished to show what they feared [c3].
chapters.kids_md: Fir'awn oppressed one group of people in his land [c2]. God told the mother of Musa to nurse her baby, and when she was afraid, to put him in the river [c4]. God promised to give him back to her and to make him one of His messengers [c4]. God put love for Musa in the hearts of those who found him [c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): the passage presents a promise made before the danger was over, and a mother asked to act on it [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md: Not established in the ayat: the name of Musa's mother, the name of the river (the ayat say yamm, 'the river' or 'the sea'), the date, the number of years of the oppression, and the name or dynasty of Fir'awn. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the personal names of Musa's mother and sister, the name of the river, and any dates. The sentence at 28:6 says Haman; the Quran gives no further detail on his office.

claims.statement_en: The family of Fir'awn picked him up so that he would become to them an enemy and a grief; God says Fir'awn, Haman and their soldiers were sinners.
The wife of Fir'awn said “A joy of the eye for me and for you; do not kill him; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son”, and they did not perceive.
The heart of Musa's mother became empty; she was about to disclose it had God not strengthened her heart so that she would be among the believers.
She told his sister to follow him; the sister watched him from a distance while they did not perceive.
God had forbidden wet-nurses to him beforehand; the sister said “Shall I direct you to a household who will take care of him for you and be sincere to him?”
God returned him to his mother so that her eye would be cooled and she would not grieve, and so that she would know that God's promise is true.
Later, Fir'awn said to Musa “Did we not raise you among us as a child, and you stayed among us for years of your life?”

chapters.summary_md: The family of Fir'awn picked him up [c1], and Fir'awn's wife said not to kill him [c2]. His mother's heart was emptied and God strengthened it [c3]. His sister followed him [c4], asked whether she could direct them to a household to nurse him [c5], and God returned him to his mother [c6]. Fir'awn later reminded Musa that he had been raised among them [c7].
chapters.body_md: The family of Fir'awn picked up the child so that he would become to them an enemy and a grief [c1]. The wife of Fir'awn said he was a joy of the eye for her and for Fir'awn, that they should not kill him, and that perhaps he would benefit them or be adopted as a son; they did not perceive [c2]. The heart of Musa's mother became empty, and she would nearly have disclosed him had God not strengthened her heart [c3]. She told his sister to follow him, and the sister watched from a distance while they did not perceive [c4]. God had forbidden wet-nurses to the child beforehand, and the sister said she could direct them to a household who would take care of him and be sincere to him [c5]. God returned him to his mother so that her eye would be cooled, she would not grieve, and she would know that God's promise is true [c6]. Another passage records Fir'awn later reminding Musa that he had been raised among them as a child and had stayed for years of his life [c7].
chapters.deep_md: Both passages end the return with the mother's eye cooled and no more grief [c6]. Only one gives the words of the sister and of the wife [c2][c5]. God says the family picked him up so that he would become to them an enemy [c1], and the next sentence gives the wife's words about a joy of the eye [c2]; the text records both without reconciling them.
chapters.kids_md: Fir'awn's family found the baby [c1]. Fir'awn's wife said not to kill him, since he might be a benefit to them [c2]. Musa's sister watched from far away and asked whether she could find someone to care for him [c4][c5]. So God gave Musa back to his mother, so that she would not grieve [c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): the account shows the mother's fear and God's strengthening of her heart [c3], and a promise kept [c6]. It also records a good word from an unexpected person in the palace of an unjust ruler [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md: Not established in the ayat: the names of the wife of Fir'awn (Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text), of Musa's sister, and of the nursing household; the length of time; where in Fir'awn's household he lived (the ayat do not describe a building; this draft does not say palace). Whether the ‘years’ in 26:18 refers to this period or a longer one is not stated.

claims.statement_en: When he reached his full strength and was established, God gave him judgement and knowledge.

He entered the city at a time of heedlessness of its people and found a pair of men fighting, one from his party and one from his enemy; the one from his party asked him for help against the one from his enemy; Musa struck him and ended his life.
Musa said “This is of the work of Satan; he is a manifest misleading enemy.”
He said “My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me”, and God forgave him; and he said “My Lord, for the favour You have shown me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals.”
In the morning he was in the city fearful and watching; the one who had asked for his help the day before cried out to him again, and Musa said to him “You are clearly a deviant.”

When he wished to seize the one who was an enemy to both of them, a speaker said “Musa, do you want to kill me as you killed a person yesterday? You only want to be a tyrant in the land and do not want to be among the reformers.”
A man came running from the far end of the city and said “Musa, the chiefs are conspiring about you to kill you, so leave; I am to you one of the sincere advisers.”
He left fearful and watching, and said “My Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people.”

Musa was later told “You did your deed which you did, and you were of the ungrateful”; he replied “I did it then while I was among those who erred; I fled from you when I feared you; then my Lord gave me judgement and made me one of the messengers.”
God reminds Musa that he killed a person and God delivered him from distress and tried him with trials.

chapters.summary_md: Musa was given judgement and knowledge [c1]. In the city he struck a man who died [c2], called it the work of Satan, and asked forgiveness [c3][c4]. Next morning he was warned that the chiefs were conspiring to kill him [c7], and he left, asking to be saved from the wrongdoing people [c8].
chapters.body_md:
When Musa reached his full strength, God gave him judgement and knowledge [c1]. He entered the city when its people were heedless and found a pair of men fighting; the one from his party asked for his help against his enemy, Musa struck the other, and ended his life [c2]. He said it was of the work of Satan, a manifest misleading enemy [c3], and asked his Lord to forgive him, which God did; he said he would never be a supporter of the criminals [c4].

In the morning he was fearful and watching; the man who had asked for his help the day before cried out again, and Musa called him a clear deviant [c5]. As Musa wished to seize the one who was an enemy to both, a speaker said he wanted to be a tyrant and not a reformer, asking if he meant to kill as he had killed the day before [c6]. A man came running from the far end of the city with a warning that the chiefs were conspiring to kill him, and told him to leave [c7]. Musa left, fearful and watching, and asked to be saved from the wrongdoing people [c8].

Musa was later told that he had done his deed and was of the ungrateful, and he answered that he did it when he erred, fled from fear, and that his Lord then gave him judgement and made him a messenger [c9]. Another passage recalls that God delivered him from distress and tried him with trials [c10].
chapters.deep_md: The killing and the fear are recorded in more than one passage [c2][c9][c10]. One gives the sequence of the days [c2][c5], the prayer for forgiveness and the forgiveness [c4], and the running man [c7]. Musa's own account of it is brief and ties the flight to fear [c9]. The first act is called the work of Satan [c3], and Musa calls himself one who wronged himself [c4].
chapters.kids_md: One day in the city Musa tried to help a man, and a fight ended in a man's death [c2]. Musa said he had wronged himself and asked God to forgive him, and God forgave him [c4]. A man ran to warn him that the chiefs wanted to harm him, and Musa left the city and asked God to save him [c7][c8].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): the account records a prophet admitting a wrong, asking for forgiveness, and being forgiven [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md: Not established in the ayat: which of the pair men is meant by ‘from his party’ and ‘from his enemy’ beyond those words, the name of the city, who spoke in 28:19 (interpreters differ), how Musa struck the man, the name of the man who warned him (Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text), and the length of the interval between the events. Another passage 26:20 uses a word that interpreters render in different ways (‘erred’, ‘was unaware’); this draft gives one rendering for review.

claims.statement_en: As he turned toward Madyan he said “Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way.”

At the water of Madyan he found a group of people watering and, apart from them, a pair of women holding back; he asked “What is your affair?” and they said “We cannot water until the shepherds leave, and our father is an old man.”
He watered for them, withdrew to the shade, and said “My Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me.”

One of the pair came to him walking shyly and said “My father invites you to pay you the reward for watering for us”; when he came to the father and told him his story, the father said “Do not fear; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people.”
One of the pair said “Father, hire him; the best you can hire is the strong, the trustworthy.”

The father said he wished to marry one of his daughters here to him on condition that he serve him for eight years, and that if he completed ten it would be from him; he did not wish to burden him, and Musa would find him, if God willed, among the righteous.
Musa said “That is between me and you; whichever of the pair terms I complete, there is no injustice to me; and God is a witness over what we say.”
Another passage says he stayed for years among the people of Madyan and then came at a decreed time.

chapters.summary_md: Musa turned toward Madyan [c1], helped a pair of women at the water [c2][c3], was invited by their father [c4], and was offered a marriage in return for service for eight years, with ten as a favour [c6]. He accepted the terms [c7]. Another passage says he stayed years among the people of Madyan [c8].
chapters.body_md:
As Musa turned toward Madyan he said he hoped his Lord would guide him to the right way [c1]. At the water he found people watering and a pair of women holding back; they told him they could not water until the shepherds left and that their father was an old man [c2]. He watered for them, withdrew to the shade, and said he was in need of whatever good God would send to him [c3]. One of them came shyly to invite him from her father to be paid for the watering; the father, hearing his story, told him not to fear for he had escaped the wrongdoing people [c4]. One said her father should hire him as the strong and trustworthy [c5].

The father offered to marry him to one of his daughters here in return for eight years of service, with ten as a favour from Musa if he completed them [c6]. Musa agreed to the terms and made God a witness [c7]. Another passage says Musa stayed for years among the people of Madyan and then came at a decreed time [c8].
chapters.deep_md: The passage gives the details of an ordinary agreement: the work, the term and the marriage [c6][c7]. The terms are a choice of lengths, with the longer a favour [c6], and Musa's reply refers to both lengths [c7]. The prayer in the shade is the only speech of Musa to God recorded between the flight and the fire in this passage [c3].
chapters.kids_md: Musa came to the water of Madyan and saw a pair of women who could not get water for their sheep [c2]. He helped them [c2][c3]. Later their father offered him a marriage if he served for years, and Musa agreed [c6][c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): Musa helps without being asked and then asks God for good [c3]. The father's offer is made with a plain statement of terms [c6], and the daughter describes a good worker as strong and trustworthy [c5].
chapters.unknowns_md: Not established in the ayat: the name of the father and of his daughters; whether the father was a prophet (Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: a name linking him to Shu'ayb, whom the Quran elsewhere sends to Madyan, but the ayat here do not make that link); the location of Madyan; which of the pair terms Musa completed (the ayat say only that he completed the term, 28:29); and the name of the daughter he married.

claims.statement_en: When Musa had completed the term and set out with his family, he perceived a fire on the side of the mountain (at-Tur) and said to his family “Stay here; I have perceived a fire; perhaps I will bring you news from it, or a burning brand from the fire so that you may warm yourselves.”
When he came to it he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, from the tree: “Musa, I am God, the Lord of the worlds.”
In another passage, he was called “Musa, I am your Lord, so take off your sandals; you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa.”
He was told “I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed; I am God, there is no god but Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance.”

He was told that the Hour is coming, which God almost keeps hidden, so that every soul is recompensed for its striving, and not to let the one who does not believe in it and follows his desire turn him from it.
In another passage, the call says “Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it, and glory be to God, Lord of the worlds. Musa, it is I, God, the Almighty, the Wise.”
Another passage asks whether the account of Musa has reached the listener, when his Lord called him in the sacred valley of Tuwa.
A further passage says of Musa that he was chosen (mukhlas), a messenger and a prophet; that God called him from the right side of the mountain (at-Tur) and brought him near in private converse.

chapters.summary_md: On the way with his family Musa saw a fire and went to bring news or a brand from it [c1]. He was called from the valley, “I am God, the Lord of the worlds” [c2], told to take off his sandals [c3], told that he was chosen, to worship God and establish prayer [c4], and told of the coming Hour [c5]. Other passages say that his Lord called him in the sacred valley of Tuwa [c7], and that he was chosen, a messenger and a prophet, brought near in private converse [c8].
chapters.body_md:
Musa, having completed the term and set out with his family, perceived a fire on the side of the mountain and told his family to stay while he went to bring news from it or a burning brand [c1]. As he came to it, he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, from the tree: “Musa, I am God, the Lord of the worlds” [c2]. The call also says “I am your Lord, so take off your sandals; you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa” [c3]. He was told that he was chosen and should listen to what is revealed, that God is God, there is no god but Him, and to worship Him and establish prayer for His remembrance [c4], and that the Hour is coming [c5]. Another passage adds the call “Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it” and “Musa, it is I, God, the Almighty, the Wise” [c6].

Another passage asks whether the account of Musa has reached the listener, when his Lord called him in the sacred valley of Tuwa [c7]. A further passage says he was chosen, a messenger and a prophet, that God called him from the right side of the mountain and brought him near in private converse [c8].
chapters.deep_md: The passages agree on the fire [c1], the valley [c3] and the call by name [c2][c3][c6]. The call is described as coming from the tree [c2], and the ayat say no more about the tree. Some of what Musa was told is given in separate passages: the identity of the caller [c2][c6], the command to take off his sandals [c3], the central message of worship and prayer [c4], and the coming Hour [c5]. Other passages add to this: one opens with a question to the listener [c7], and one describes Musa as chosen, a messenger and a prophet who was brought near in private converse [c8].
chapters.kids_md: Musa saw a fire and went toward it to bring his family some news or a piece of it to warm them [c1]. A voice called out: “Musa, I am God, the Lord of the worlds” [c2]. God told him to take off his sandals because he was in a holy valley [c3]. God told him to worship Him and to pray [c4]. Musa was a messenger and a prophet whom God called and brought near [c8].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): the message Musa received first is about worship and prayer [c4], with a reminder of the coming Hour [c5].
chapters.unknowns_md: Not established in the ayat: the exact place or the date, what the fire was, what the tree was, which night, and the names of those with him. The ayat say his family and do not list them. The caller's voice is described only as a call. Whether whoever is in the fire names a specific being is read differently by interpreters; this draft makes no claim. The word rendered chosen in 19:51 (mukhlas) is read as mukhlis, one who is sincere, in a variant reading; the page should state which reading it follows.

chapters.title_en: The staff, the hand and Harun

claims.statement_en: God asked “What is that in your right hand, Musa?” and he said “It is my staff; I lean on it, I beat down leaves with it for my sheep, and I have other uses for it.”
He was told to throw it, and it became a moving snake; he was told “Take it and do not fear; we will return it to its first state.”

In another passage, and another passage, when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned in flight and did not look back; he was told to come forward and not to fear, that he was secure, and that the messengers do not fear in God's presence.

He was told to draw his hand to his side or put it in his bosom, and it would come out white without harm, as another sign; these are a pair of proofs from his Lord to Fir'awn and his chiefs, who were a defiantly disobedient people, among nine signs.
He was told to go to Fir'awn, who had transgressed.

Musa prayed “My Lord, expand my chest for me, ease my task for me, and loosen the knot from my tongue so that they understand my speech; appoint for me a minister from my family, Harun my brother; strengthen my back with him and let him share in my task, so that we may glorify You much and remember You much; You are ever seeing us.” God said “You have been given your request, Musa.”

In another passage, he said “My Lord, I killed a person among them, so I fear they will kill me; my brother Harun is more fluent than I in speech, so send him with me as support to confirm me; I fear they will deny me.”
God said “We will strengthen your arm with your brother and give you both authority so that they cannot reach you; with Our signs, both of you and those who follow you will be the victors.”
A further passage says that out of His mercy God gave Musa his brother Harun as a prophet.
The ayah after the reassurance in 27:10 makes an exception: except for one who did wrong and then replaced it, after evil, with good; for such, God says, He is Forgiving, Merciful.

chapters.summary_md: Musa was asked about what was in his hand and answered it was his staff [c1]. It became a moving snake and then was returned to its first state [c2]; he was told not to fear [c3]. His hand came out white as another sign [c4]. He was sent to Fir'awn [c5] and prayed for ease, and for Harun to be with him [c6][c7]. God said He would strengthen his arm with his brother [c8]. Another passage says that out of His mercy God gave Musa his brother Harun as a prophet [c9].
chapters.body_md:
God asked Musa what was in his right hand, and he said it was his staff, on which he leaned and with which he beat down leaves for his sheep, with other uses besides [c1]. He was told to throw it, and it became a moving snake; he was told to take it without fear, for it would return to its first state [c2]. In other passages he turned in flight and was told to come forward, that he was secure, and that messengers do not fear in God's presence [c3]. He was told to put his hand into his bosom, and it would come out white without harm, as another sign, among nine signs to Fir'awn and his people, who were defiantly disobedient [c4]. He was told to go to Fir'awn, who had transgressed [c5].

Musa then prayed for his chest to be expanded, his task eased, the knot loosened from his tongue so that they would understand his speech, and for Harun his brother as a minister to strengthen his back and share in his task; God answered that his request was granted [c6]. Another passage gives the reason: he had killed a person among them and feared being killed, and Harun was more fluent in speech [c7]. God said He would strengthen his arm with his brother and give both authority, so that they could not be reached, and they and their followers would be the victors [c8].

Another passage adds that out of His mercy God gave Musa his brother Harun as a prophet [c9]. The ayah after the reassurance to the messengers makes an exception, for one who did wrong and then replaced it with good after evil, and says that God is Forgiving, Merciful [c10].
chapters.deep_md: The staff and the hand are told in separate passages with different emphasis [c1][c3][c4]. One has the question about the staff and the gentle command to take the snake [c1][c2]; others have Musa's flight and the reassurance [c3]. The request for Harun is given as a prayer for ease and a helper [c6] and as a reason of the killing and fluency [c7], and God's answer speaks of authority and victory [c8]. The signs are called nine signs and proofs [c4]; the ayat in this draft do not list the nine. The ayah that follows the reassurance in 27:10 begins with an exception, and how the exception relates to what comes before it is read in more than one way [c10].
chapters.kids_md: God asked Musa what he held, and he said it was his staff [c1]. God told him to throw it, and it became a moving snake [c2]. Then God told him not to be afraid [c3]. God gave him another sign with his hand [c4]. Musa asked God to make his task easy and to send his brother Harun to help him, and God granted his request [c6][c8]. God also gave Musa his brother Harun as a prophet [c9].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): Musa does not simply accept the task; he asks for ease, for clearer speech, and for his brother's help [c6].
chapters.unknowns_md: Not established in these ayat: what the nine signs are, since the plagues are listed elsewhere and are not assumed to be the nine; what the knot in Musa's tongue was, since the ayat state only the request; the age of Harun relative to Musa; and where Harun was when he was sent for. The grammar of the exception in 27:11, and whom it refers to, is discussed by interpreters; this draft states the words and draws no conclusion about Musa or anyone else.

claims.statement_en: God told Musa and his brother to go with His signs and not slacken in remembering Him, to go to Fir'awn who had transgressed, and to speak to him a gentle word, so that perhaps he would remember or fear.
They said “Our Lord, we fear that he will hasten against us or transgress”; God said “Do not fear; I am with you both, hearing and seeing.”

In another passage, God called Musa to go to the wrongdoing people, the people of Fir'awn, asking “Will they not be mindful?”; Musa said “My Lord, I fear that they will deny me, my chest is straitened and my tongue is not fluent, so send for Harun; they also have a charge against me, so I fear they will kill me”; God said “No; go both of you with Our signs; we are with you, listening.”

They were to say to Fir'awn “We are a pair of messengers of your Lord (the messenger of the Lord of the worlds): send the Children of Israel with us and do not torment them; we have come to you with a sign from your Lord; peace be upon the one who follows the guidance.”

Fir'awn said “Did we not raise you among us as a child, and you stayed among us for years of your life? And you did your deed which you did, and you were of the ungrateful.” Musa said that he had done it then while he erred, fled when he feared, and was then given judgement and made one of the messengers.
Musa said “That is a favour you hold over me: that you have enslaved the Children of Israel.” (Interpreters read this sentence as a statement or as a question.)

Fir'awn asked “Who is your Lord, Musa?” and Musa said “Our Lord is He who gave everything its form and then guided.” Fir'awn asked about the earlier generations and Musa said their knowledge is with his Lord in a record; his Lord neither errs nor forgets.

In another passage, Fir'awn asked “And what is the Lord of the worlds?” Musa answered “The Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, if you are convinced”, then “Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers”, then “The Lord of the east and the west and what is between them, if you use reason.”
Fir'awn said to those around him “Do you not hear?” and said “Your messenger who was sent to you is surely mad.”
Fir'awn said “If you take a god other than me, I will make you one of the imprisoned.” Musa said “Even if I bring you something clear?” Fir'awn said “Bring it, if you are of the truthful.”
Another passage says Musa was told to go to Fir'awn, who had transgressed, and to say “Would you be purified, and shall I guide you to your Lord so that you fear?”

chapters.summary_md: Musa and Harun were sent to Fir'awn with a gentle word [c1], having voiced their fear and been told God was with them [c2][c3]. Their message was to send the Children of Israel with them [c4]. Fir'awn reminded Musa of the years in his household [c5], asked who the Lord is [c7][c8], called Musa mad [c9] and threatened prison [c10]. Another passage adds the question whether Fir'awn would be purified [c11].
chapters.body_md:
God told Musa and his brother to go to Fir'awn with His signs, not to slacken in remembering Him, and to speak a gentle word so that perhaps Fir'awn would remember or fear [c1]. They said they feared he would hasten against them or transgress, and God said He was with them, hearing and seeing [c2]. In another passage Musa voiced fear of being denied, his tongue not being fluent, and a charge against him, and asked that Harun be sent for; God said to go with His signs and that He was listening [c3].

The message was that they were messengers and that Fir'awn should send the Children of Israel with them and not torment them, with peace on the one who follows the guidance [c4]. Fir'awn answered by recalling the years Musa stayed with them and his deed, and Musa replied that he had done it while he erred, fled from fear, and was given judgement and made a messenger [c5]. Musa said the favour Fir'awn held over him was that he had enslaved the Children of Israel [c6].

Fir'awn asked who the Lord is; in another passage Musa answered that He gave everything its form and then guided, and that the knowledge of earlier generations is with his Lord in a record [c7]. In another passage he answered with the Lord of the heavens and the earth, of the forefathers, and of the east and the west [c8]. Fir'awn asked those around if they heard and called Musa mad [c9], then threatened to imprison him if he took a god other than Fir'awn; Musa asked if he would do so even if he brought something clear [c10]. Another passage records the instruction to go to Fir'awn, who had transgressed, and to ask whether he would be purified and offer to guide him to his Lord so that he would fear [c11].
chapters.deep_md: The meeting is told in more than one passage, each keeping a part of the exchange [c1][c3][c8]. One has the instruction to speak gently and God's assurance [c1][c2]. Another has Musa's fears [c3], Fir'awn's reminder of his upbringing and deed [c5][c6], and the series of questions [c8]. Fir'awn's statements about Musa, that he is mad [c9] and that he would imprison him [c10], are in one passage only. The question whether Fir'awn would be purified, with the offer of guidance, is in one passage only [c11].
chapters.kids_md: God told Musa and Harun to speak to Fir'awn kindly [c1]. They were a little afraid, and God told them He was with them, hearing and seeing [c1][c2]. They asked Fir'awn to let the Children of Israel go with them [c4]. Fir'awn asked who their Lord was, and Musa said He is the one who gave everything its shape and then guided it [c7]. God also told Musa to ask Fir'awn whether he would be purified, and to offer to guide him to his Lord [c11].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): the instruction to a messenger facing a tyrant is to speak a gentle word first [c1], and the assurance given to the frightened is that God is hearing and seeing [c2].
chapters.unknowns_md: Not established in the ayat: where the meeting took place, how many times it happened, which passage describes the first meeting, and the personal name or period of this Fir'awn. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: any identification with a named ruler of Egypt. The Arabic wording of 20:50, rendered here gave everything its form, has more than one possible rendering for scholarly review. How the instruction in 79:17-19 relates to the other passages of this chapter is not stated.

claims.statement_en: God sent Musa with His signs to Fir'awn and his chiefs; Musa said “Fir'awn, I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds, bound to say nothing about God but the truth; I have come to you with clear proof from your Lord, so send the Children of Israel with me.”
Fir'awn said “If you have come with a sign, bring it, if you are of the truthful.” Musa threw his staff and it was a clear serpent; he drew out his hand and it was white to the onlookers.

The chiefs said “This is a learned magician who wants to drive you out of your land”, and Fir'awn asked what they advise; they said to delay him and his brother and send gatherers into the cities to bring every learned magician.

God sent Musa and Harun to Fir'awn and his chiefs; they were arrogant and a criminal people; when the truth came, they said “This is clear magic”, and Musa said “Do you say this of the truth when it has come to you? Is this magic? The magicians do not succeed.”
They said “Have you come to turn us from what we found our fathers following, so that greatness in the land may be yours? We are not believers in both of you.”
They said “Shall we believe a pair of humans like ourselves, whose people are servants to us?”, denied them, and were among the destroyed.

They said “This is nothing but forged magic, and we never heard of this among our earlier forefathers”; Musa said “My Lord knows best who comes with guidance from Him and who will have the final home; the wrongdoers do not succeed.”

Fir'awn said “O chiefs, I do not know of any god for you other than me; so kindle for me, Haman, a fire upon clay and build me a tower so that I may look at the God of Musa; I think he is one of the liars.”

In another passage, Musa was sent with signs and clear authority to Fir'awn, Haman and Qarun, who said “a magician, a liar”; when he brought the truth they said to kill the sons of those who believed with him and keep their women alive.

Fir'awn said “Let me kill Musa and let him call upon his Lord; I fear that he will change your religion or cause corruption to appear in the land.” Musa said “I seek refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Account.”

A believing man from the family of Fir'awn, who was concealing his faith, asked “Would you kill a man because he says ‘My Lord is God’, when he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord? If he is a liar, his lie is upon him; if he is truthful, some of what he promises will strike you.”

Another passage says that Musa showed him the greatest sign, and he denied and disobeyed, then turned away striving, gathered and called out, and said “I am your lord, the most high”; God seized him with the punishment (nakal) of the last and the first; in that is a lesson for whoever fears.
