chapters.summary_md: Musa brought clear proof and asked Fir'awn to send the Children of Israel with him [c1]. He showed the staff and the hand [c2]. The chiefs called it magic and proposed gathering magicians [c3][c4]. Fir'awn claimed a position no other god was known to the chiefs [c8] and spoke of killing Musa [c10]; a believer from his family spoke against it [c11]. Another passage says that he denied the greatest sign, claimed to be the most high lord, and was seized by God [c12].
chapters.body_md:
Musa told Fir'awn that he was a messenger from the Lord of the worlds, bound to say only the truth, with clear proof, and asked him to send the Children of Israel with him [c1]. Fir'awn said to bring a sign if he was truthful; Musa threw his staff and it was a clear serpent, and his hand came out white to the onlookers [c2]. The chiefs said he was a learned magician who wanted to drive them out of the land, and advised gathering every learned magician [c3].

Another passage says that when the truth came they called it clear magic, and Musa asked how they could call it magic when magicians do not succeed [c4]; they replied that he came to turn them from their fathers' way and to gain greatness in the land [c5]. Another passage records them saying they would not believe a pair of humans like themselves whose people served them [c6]. Another passage records the answer ‘forged magic’ and Musa's reply that his Lord knows best who brings guidance [c7], and Fir'awn's saying that he knew no god for the chiefs but himself and his order to Haman to build a tower [c8]. Another passage names Fir'awn, Haman and Qarun, who said ‘a magician, a liar’, and ordered the killing of the sons of the believers [c9]. Fir'awn said he wished to kill Musa, fearing for their religion; Musa sought refuge in his Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Account [c10]. A believing man from Fir'awn's family concealing his faith asked whether they would kill a man for saying ‘My Lord is God’ [c11].

Another passage says Musa showed him the greatest sign, and he denied and disobeyed, turned away striving, gathered and called out that he was their lord, the most high; God seized him with the punishment of the last and the first, and in that is a lesson for whoever fears [c12].
chapters.deep_md: The passages share one pattern: a sign is shown and called magic [c2][c4][c7][c9], those in authority respond with fear of loss of land and ancestral ways [c3][c5][c10], and Fir'awn makes a claim for himself [c8]. One passage adds a figure not seen elsewhere in this draft, a believing man in Fir'awn's own family [c11]. The passage that ends with a lesson for whoever fears [c12] is the only one in this chapter that tells how Fir'awn was seized.
chapters.kids_md: Musa showed Fir'awn the signs God gave him [c2]. Fir'awn and his chiefs said it was magic [c4][c7]. Fir'awn said he knew of no god for them but himself [c8]. One man in Fir'awn's family secretly believed, and he asked whether they would kill a man for saying that his Lord is God [c11]. Fir'awn denied the greatest sign and God seized him, and there is a lesson in that for whoever fears [c12].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): the account notes that clear signs can be explained away by those who fear to lose position [c3][c5], and that a single voice from inside such a court spoke in defence of what was right [c11].
chapters.unknowns_md: Not established in the ayat: the time and place of each meeting with the court, how many conversations there were, the identity and name of the believing man (Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text), and who Qarun and Haman were beyond what is said in the ayat. The phrase the punishment of the last and the first in 79:25 is read in more than one way by interpreters (for example the Hereafter and this world, or his last and his first saying); this draft states the words and does not choose.

claims.statement_en: In another passage, Fir'awn said “Have you come to drive us out of our land with your magic, Musa? We will bring you magic like it; so set an appointment between us and you, which neither we nor you shall fail, at a place midway.” Musa said “Your appointment is the day of the festival, and let the people be gathered at forenoon.”
Fir'awn turned away, gathered his plan, then came; Musa said to them “Woe to you, do not invent a lie against God, lest He destroy you with a punishment; whoever invents has failed.”
The magicians were gathered for the appointed time of a known day, and the people were asked whether they would gather, so that they might follow the magicians if they were the victors.
The magicians asked Fir'awn whether they would have a reward if they were the victors; he said “Yes, and you will then be among those brought near.”
They said “Musa, either you throw, or we will be the ones to throw”; he said “Throw.” when they threw, they bewitched the people and terrified them and brought great magic.

Their ropes and staffs seemed to Musa, from their magic, to be moving, and Musa felt fear within himself; God said “Do not fear; you are the uppermost. Throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow what they have made; what they have made is only the trick of a magician, and the magician does not succeed wherever he comes.”
Musa threw his staff and it swallowed what they fabricated; the truth was established and what they were doing was made void, and they were defeated there and turned back humbled.

In another passage, Musa said to the magicians “Throw what you will throw”, and after they threw, “What you have brought is magic; God will make it vain; God does not set right the work of the corrupters; and God establishes the truth by His words, even if the criminals dislike it.”
The magicians were cast down in prostration, and said “We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun” (another passage has “the Lord of Harun and Musa”).

Fir'awn said “You believed him before I gave you permission? He is your chief who taught you magic. I will cut off your hands and feet on opposite sides and I will crucify you all.” (another passage says on the trunks of palm trees.)

They said “No harm; to our Lord we will return; we hope that our Lord will forgive us our faults because we were the first of the believers”, and “You take revenge on us only because we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us. Our Lord, pour patience upon us and take us in death as Muslims.”

In another passage, they said “We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that came to us and over Him who created us; so decree whatever you decree; you only decree for this worldly life. We have believed in our Lord so that He may forgive us our faults and the magic to which you compelled us; God is better and more lasting.”

In another passage, they disputed their affair among themselves and kept their private talk secret; they said “These are a pair of magicians who want to drive you out of your land by their magic and do away with your best way. So gather your plan, then come in a line; whoever has the upper hand today has succeeded.”
In another passage, Musa said to them “Throw what you are going to throw”; they threw their ropes and staffs and said “By the might of Fir'awn, we are the victors.”

chapters.summary_md: A day was set for Musa and the magicians [c1][c3]. They disputed among themselves and spoke of a pair of magicians who wanted to drive them out [c13]. The magicians threw first [c5], after Musa told them to throw what they were going to throw, and they spoke of the might of Fir'awn [c14] and it seemed to Musa that their ropes moved [c6]. His staff swallowed what they had made [c7]. The magicians fell down in prostration and said they believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun [c9]. Fir'awn threatened them [c10], and they answered with patience and hope for forgiveness [c11][c12].
chapters.body_md:
Fir'awn proposed an appointment between his magicians and Musa, and Musa set the day of the festival, with the people gathered at forenoon [c1]. Fir'awn gathered his plan and came; Musa warned them not to invent a lie against God [c2]. They disputed among themselves, kept their talk secret, and said that this was a pair of magicians who wanted to drive them out of their land and do away with their best way, and told one another to gather their plan and come in a line, for whoever had the upper hand that day had succeeded [c13]. The people were asked to gather in case the magicians won [c3], and the magicians asked for a reward, which Fir'awn promised, with nearness to him [c4]. They asked whether Musa would throw first; he told them to throw, and they bewitched the people and brought great magic [c5]. In another passage Musa told them to throw what they were going to throw; they threw their ropes and staffs and said that by the might of Fir'awn they were the victors [c14]. Their ropes and staffs seemed to move and Musa felt fear within himself; God told him not to fear, that he was uppermost, and to throw what was in his right hand [c6]. His staff swallowed what they had fabricated, the truth was established and they were defeated [c7]. Another passage gives Musa's words after they threw: that God will make it vain and establishes the truth by His words [c8].

The magicians were cast down in prostration, saying “We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun” [c9]. Fir'awn said they had believed before his permission, that Musa was their chief who taught them magic, and that he would cut off their hands and feet on opposite sides and crucify them [c10]. They answered that there was no harm, that they would return to their Lord and hoped for forgiveness [c11], and in another passage that they would not prefer him over the clear proofs and over Him who created them [c12].
chapters.deep_md: The day of the magicians is told in more than one passage, with a parallel structure [c1][c5][c9]. One has the scene-setting by Fir'awn and Musa [c1][c2] and Musa's fear [c6]. Others have the reward and the dialogue of the magicians [c4][c5] and the swallowing [c7]. The words of the magicians after their prostration are given in forms that agree on the Lord of the worlds [c9], with fuller responses in some [c11] and the declaration against the threat in another [c12]. The gathering of the plan in 20:64 [c13] and the cry by the might of Fir'awn in 26:44 [c14] are each in one passage only.
chapters.kids_md: Fir'awn set a day to meet Musa with his magicians [c1]. They threw their ropes and sticks, and it seemed to Musa that they were moving [c6]. God told him not to fear and to throw his staff [c6]. His staff swallowed what the magicians had made, and the magicians fell down and said they believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun [c7][c9]. The magicians threw their ropes and sticks and called on the might of Fir'awn [c14].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): the magicians were the experts of their craft, and they recognised what they saw as different from their own work [c7][c9]. They then held to their belief when threatened [c11][c12].
chapters.unknowns_md: Not established in the ayat: how many magicians there were, the place and date of the festival, the nature of their ropes and staffs beyond that they seemed to move, and whether the descriptions of the throwing describe separate moments. The fate of the magicians after the threat is not narrated. Who is meant by they in 20:62-64 is not marked in the ayat; the reading and grammar of 20:63 (a pair of magicians) are discussed by scholars.

claims.statement_en: The chiefs asked Fir'awn “Will you leave Musa and his people to spread corruption in the land and leave you and your gods?” he said “We will kill their sons and keep their women alive, and we are dominant over them.”
Musa said to his people “Seek help in God and be patient; the earth is God's; he gives it as an inheritance to whom He wills of His servants; and the end is for the mindful.”
They said “We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us.” he said “Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land, and then see how you act.”

God seized the people of Fir'awn with years of drought and a shortage of fruits, so that they might remember; when good came they said it was theirs, and when evil struck they blamed Musa and those with him as an omen; God says their omen is with Him.
They said “Whatever sign you bring to bewitch us with, we will not believe you.”
God sent upon them the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood as detailed signs; they were arrogant and a criminal people.

When the plague fell on them they said “Musa, call upon your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you; if you remove the plague from us, we will believe you and send the Children of Israel with you”; when God removed it for a term which they were to reach, they broke their word.
None believed Musa except some of the offspring (dhurriyyah) of his people, in fear that Fir'awn and his chiefs would persecute them; Fir'awn was high in the land and among the transgressors.

Musa said “My people, if you have believed in God, then rely upon Him, if you are Muslims”; they said “In God we put our trust. Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people, and save us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people.”

God inspired Musa and his brother to settle their people in houses in Misr, to make their houses a qiblah (the Arabic word qiblah is left untranslated here), to establish prayer, and to give good news to the believers.

Musa said “Our Lord, You gave Fir'awn and his chiefs adornment and wealth in the life of this world; our Lord, that they may lead astray from Your way; our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts, so that they do not believe until they see the painful punishment.” God said “Your supplication has been answered, so be upright and do not follow the way of those who do not know.”

chapters.summary_md: Fir'awn's chiefs urged him against Musa and his people, and he said he would kill their sons [c1]. Musa told his people to seek God's help and be patient [c2]. A drought and a shortage of fruits [c4] and the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood [c6] came on Fir'awn's people. They promised to believe if relieved and broke their word [c7]. Only some of the offspring of his people believed, in fear [c8]; Musa and his brother were told to settle their people in houses and establish prayer [c10].
chapters.body_md:
The chiefs asked Fir'awn if he would leave Musa and his people to spread corruption and abandon him and his gods, and he said he would kill their sons and keep their women alive [c1]. Musa told his people to seek help in God and be patient, because the earth is God's and He gives it to whom He wills [c2]. They said they had been harmed before and after he came; he said that perhaps their Lord would destroy their enemy and make them successors, and see how they would act [c3].

God seized Fir'awn's people with years of drought and shortage of fruit so that they would remember; they credited good to themselves and blamed Musa and those with him for evil, and God says their omen is with Him [c4]. They said no sign would make them believe [c5]. God sent the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood as detailed signs, and they were arrogant [c6]. When the plague fell they asked Musa to call upon his Lord, promising to believe and to send the Children of Israel; when it was removed they broke their word [c7].

Another passage says none believed Musa except some of the offspring (dhurriyyah) of his people, for fear of Fir'awn [c8]. Musa told them to rely upon God, and they said they trusted in God and asked not to be a trial for the wrongdoers and to be saved [c9]. God inspired Musa and his brother to settle their people in houses in Misr, to establish prayer and to give good news to the believers [c10]. Musa prayed about Fir'awn's adornment and wealth, and God said his supplication had been answered and told them to be upright [c11].
chapters.deep_md: One passage records the pressure and the signs [c1][c4][c6][c7]; another records the limited number of believers and their prayers [c8][c9][c11]. The signs listed in the first are not claimed to be those mentioned elsewhere [c6]. The Arabic word dhurriyyah in [c8], offspring or descendants, is understood in more than one way by interpreters.
chapters.kids_md: Fir'awn's chiefs urged him against Musa and his people [c1]. Musa told them to ask God for help and to be patient [c2]. God sent signs to Fir'awn's people so that they would remember [c4][c6]. They promised to believe if the trouble stopped, but when it stopped they did not keep their word [c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): the account shows a promise made in hardship and broken in ease [c7]. It also shows a small group asking God for protection and trust in Him [c9].
chapters.unknowns_md: Not established in the ayat: the order, length and number of the plagues beyond those named in 7:133; how many believed; who the dhurriyyah were, since the ayat say offspring of his people; and the meaning of making houses a qiblah in 10:87, where interpreters differ.

claims.statement_en: God inspired Musa and told him “Travel by night with My servants; you will be pursued.”
Fir'awn sent gatherers into the cities, and said “These are a small band; they enrage us; and we are all on guard.”
God took the people of Fir'awn out of gardens, springs, treasures and a noble station, and gave it as an inheritance to the Children of Israel.
They pursued them at sunrise; when the pair of hosts saw each other, the companions of Musa said “We are about to be overtaken”; he said “No; my Lord is with me; he will guide me.”
God inspired Musa and said “Strike the sea with your staff”; it split, and each part was like a great mountain.

In another passage, God told him to strike for them a dry path in the sea, fearing neither being overtaken nor any other danger; Fir'awn followed them with his soldiers and the sea covered them with what covered them.
God brought the others near, saved Musa and all who were with him, and then drowned the others; in that is a sign, and most of them were not believers.
God says that He parted the sea for them and saved them and drowned the family of Fir'awn while they were watching.

God says that He took the Children of Israel across the sea, and Fir'awn and his soldiers followed in transgression and enmity; when drowning overtook him he said “I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of the Muslims.”

He was told “Now? While you disobeyed before and were among the corrupters? Today We will save you in your body, so that you may be a sign for those who come after you; many people are heedless of Our signs.”

Fir'awn and his soldiers were arrogant in the land without right and thought they would not be returned to God; God seized him and his soldiers and cast them into the sea, made them leaders calling to the Fire, followed them with a curse in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised.
Fir'awn wished to drive them from the land, and God drowned him and those with him all together.

Another passage says that Musa was told to leave the sea calm (the word rendered calm, rahwan, is read in more than one way), for they were a host to be drowned; and that God saved the Children of Israel from the humiliating punishment, from Fir'awn, who was high and among the transgressors.
Fir'awn led his people astray and did not guide them.
The ayah after the sign says: indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.

That passage also says how many gardens and springs, crops and a noble station they left, and the comfort in which they took pleasure; that God gave it as an inheritance to another people; and that neither the sky nor the earth wept over them, and they were not given respite.

chapters.summary_md: Musa was told to travel by night with God's servants and that they would be pursued [c1]. Fir'awn sent gatherers [c2]. At the sea, Musa said his Lord was with him [c4] and was told to strike it; it split [c5][c6]. Musa and those with him were saved and Fir'awn's host was drowned [c7][c8][c9]. Another passage says that God saved the Children of Israel from the humiliating punishment [c11], and that those drowned left gardens and springs behind [c16].
chapters.body_md:
God inspired Musa to travel by night with His servants and told him they would be pursued [c1]. Fir'awn sent gatherers into the cities, calling Musa's people a small band who enraged him [c2]. God says He took the people of Fir'awn out of gardens, springs, treasures and a noble station and gave it as an inheritance to the Children of Israel [c3].

They pursued at sunrise; when the pair of hosts saw each other, Musa's companions said they were about to be overtaken, and Musa said his Lord was with him and would guide him [c4]. God told him to strike the sea with his staff, and it split, each part like a great mountain [c5]. Another passage says to strike a dry path in the sea, with no fear of being overtaken, and that the sea covered Fir'awn and his soldiers [c6]. It also says that Fir'awn led his people astray and did not guide them [c14]. God brought the others near, saved Musa and all with him, and drowned the others [c7]. The ayah after the sign says that your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful [c15]. Another passage says God parted the sea and drowned the family of Fir'awn while the Children of Israel were watching [c8].

When drowning overtook Fir'awn, he said he believed that there is no god but the One in whom the Children of Israel believe; he was answered with “Now”? and told he would be saved in his body as a sign for those after him [c9][c10]. Another passage says God cast Fir'awn and his soldiers into the sea [c12]. Another passage says Fir'awn wished to drive them from the land and God drowned him and those with him together [c13].

Another passage says that Musa was told to leave the sea calm, for they were a host to be drowned, and that God saved the Children of Israel from the humiliating punishment, from Fir'awn, who was high and among the transgressors [c11]. It says how many gardens, springs, crops and a noble station they left, and the comfort in which they took pleasure, that God gave it as an inheritance to another people, and that neither the sky nor the earth wept over them and they were not given respite [c16].
chapters.deep_md: One passage gives the fullest sequence: the command, the pursuit, the fear, the sea, the rescue and the drowning [c1][c4][c5][c7]. Another says a dry path [c6]. The words saved in your body in 10:92 are stated in the text without explanation [c10]. The exchange with the drowning Fir'awn is in one passage only [c9][c10]. The ayat that name the inheritance of gardens and springs do not say it was the land spoken of in other chapters [c3]. The call to leave the sea calm [c11] and the list of what the drowned left behind [c16] are in the passage on the humiliating punishment only. The ayah that says another people inherited it [c16] does not name them, while the earlier passage names the Children of Israel as the heirs [c3].
chapters.kids_md: God told Musa to leave at night with his people [c1]. When Musa's people saw the army and the sea, they were afraid, but Musa said his Lord was with him [c4]. God told Musa to strike the sea with his staff, and it split [c5]. Musa and his people were saved [c7]. God saved the Children of Israel from Fir'awn [c11].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): the group's fear at the sea is answered by one sentence, “my Lord is with me; He will guide me” [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md: Not established in the ayat: the name or the place of the sea, which the ayat call bahr and yamm; the date; the number of people who crossed; the place on the far shore; and what God did with the body of Fir'awn beyond saving it as a sign. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: any identification of a body with a named king. The land inherited in 26:59 is not named. The word rahwan in 44:24 is read in more than one way (calm, open or parted); the draft leaves it open.

claims.statement_en: God says He shaded them with the cloud and sent down upon them al-mann and as-salwa (rendered here manna and salwa), telling them to eat of the good things He provided; they did not wrong Him, but they wronged themselves.

When Musa asked for water for his people, God told him to strike the stone with his staff, and springs gushed from it, one for each people; each people knew its drinking place; they were told to eat and drink of God's provision and not to spread corruption in the land.
God divided them into tribes, as nations.

They said “Musa, we cannot endure one kind of food, so call upon your Lord to bring forth for us of what the earth grows, its herbs, cucumbers, fum, lentils and onions” (fum is rendered by interpreters as garlic or as wheat); he said “Would you exchange what is better for what is lower? Go down to a town (misran), for you will have what you asked.”

They were told to enter a town, eat from it wherever they wished, enter the gate prostrating, and say “Hittah” so that God would forgive their mistakes; those who did wrong changed the word they had been given, and God sent a punishment (rijz) from the heaven on them.

In another passage, God recalls to the Children of Israel that He saved them from their enemy, promised them the right side of the mountain, and sent down the manna and the salwa; he warns them not to transgress in it, for His anger would descend; and says He is Forgiving to the one who repents, believes and does good and then is guided.

Musa reminded his people of God's favour, that He placed prophets among them, made them kings and gave them what He had not given anyone in the worlds, and told them to enter the holy land which God had assigned to them and not to turn back.

They said “Musa, there is a people of tyrants in it, and we will not enter until they leave; if they leave, we will enter”; a pair of men of those who feared, whom God had favoured, said “Enter upon them by the gate; when you enter it, you will be the victors; and rely upon God, if you are believers.”
They said “Musa, we will never enter it as long as they are in it; so go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are sitting here.”

Musa said “My Lord, I have power over none but myself and my brother, so separate us from the defiantly disobedient people.” God said the land would be forbidden to them for years, during which they would wander in the earth, and told Musa not to grieve over the defiantly disobedient people.

chapters.summary_md: In the wilderness the Children of Israel were shaded and given manna and salwa [c1] and water from a stone [c2]. They asked for other foods [c4]. When told to enter the holy land they refused [c8][c9], and Musa asked to be separated from them; God said the land would be forbidden for years [c10].
chapters.body_md:
God says He shaded them with the cloud and sent down the manna and the salwa, telling them to eat of the good things [c1]. When Musa asked for water for his people, he was told to strike the stone with his staff, and springs gushed forth, one for each people, each people knowing its drinking place [c2]; they were divided into tribes [c3]. They then said they could not endure one kind of food, and asked for herbs, cucumbers, fum, lentils and onions; Musa asked if they would exchange better for lower [c4]. They were told to enter a town, eat freely, enter the gate prostrating and say “Hittah”; those who did wrong changed the word and a punishment was sent from the heaven [c5]. Another passage recalls the favours and warns against transgression, while saying that God forgives the one who repents [c6].

Another passage records Musa's reminder of the favours, and the command to enter the holy land [c7]. His people said there were tyrants and that they would not enter until they left; a pair of men whom God had favoured said to enter by the gate and rely on God [c8]. His people answered that they would never enter and that Musa and his Lord should go and fight while they sat [c9]. Musa said he had power only over himself and his brother and asked to be separated from them; God said the land was forbidden to them for years while they wandered [c10].
chapters.deep_md: Provision (manna, salwa, shade, water) [c1][c2] and refusal (the foods [c4], the gate [c5], the land [c8][c9]) are interwoven in these passages without a fixed order. The word misran in [c4] can be read as a town or as the name Misr; it is flagged for review. The decree of years of wandering [c10] follows Musa's own words that he has power only over himself and his brother [c10]. The town of [c5] and the holy land of [c7] are not stated to be the same place.
chapters.kids_md: God told Musa to strike a stone, and springs came out of it [c1][c2]. Later Musa told his people to enter the holy land, but they said they would not enter until the people in it left, and that they would sit where they were [c8][c9].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): the account sets God's provision [c1][c2] beside the people's complaints [c4] and refusals [c9]. A pair of men who feared still urged trust in God [c8].
chapters.unknowns_md: Not established in the ayat: the place of the wandering, the identity of the ‘a pair of men’ in 5:23 (Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text; none is used here), the names of the tribes, the identity of the ‘town’ and the ‘holy land’ (the ayat do not name them), how the ‘punishment from the heaven’ of 2:59 took place, and whether the years began at once.

chapters.title_en: The appointed time and the tablets

claims.statement_en: God appointed thirty nights for Musa and completed them with ten, so that the appointed time of his Lord was completed; Musa said to his brother Harun “Take my place among my people, set things right, and do not follow the way of the corrupters.”
In another passage, God asked “What made you hasten from your people, Musa?” and he said “They are on my track, and I hastened to You, my Lord, so that You would be pleased.”

When Musa came at the appointed time and his Lord spoke to him, he said “My Lord, show me, that I may look at You.” God said “You will not see Me, but look at the mountain; if it stays in its place, then you will see Me.”
When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble, and Musa fell unconscious; when he recovered he said “Glory be to You; I repent to You, and I am the first of the believers.”
God said “Musa, I have chosen you over the people with My messages and My speech; so take what I have given you and be among the grateful.”
God wrote for him in the tablets (al-alwah) of everything, an admonition and a detailing of everything, and told him to take them with strength and command his people to take the best of them.

God says He will turn away from His signs those who are arrogant in the land without right, so that even if they see every sign they do not believe, and that those who denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter, their deeds are worthless.
God says that He gave Musa the Book and the Criterion (al-furqan) so that they might be guided.
When Musa's anger subsided he took up the tablets, and in what was written in them was guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord.

Musa chose seventy men of his people for God's appointment; when the quake seized them he said “My Lord, if You had willed, You could have destroyed them before, and me. Would You destroy us for what the foolish among us did? It is only Your trial, by which You lead astray whom You will and guide whom You will; You are our protector, so forgive us and have mercy on us.”

Musa asked for good in this world and the Hereafter, and said “we have turned to You”; God said His punishment strikes whom He wills, and His mercy encompasses all things, and He will write it down for those who are mindful, give zakat and believe in His signs.

chapters.summary_md: God appointed nights for Musa, and he left Harun in charge of his people [c1]. Musa asked to look at his Lord, and the mountain crumbled [c3][c4]. God told him He had chosen him with His messages and speech [c5], and wrote the tablets for him [c6]. Musa also chose seventy men for the appointment [c10].
chapters.body_md:
God appointed thirty nights for Musa and completed them with ten, so that the appointed time was completed; Musa told Harun to take his place and set things right [c1]. In another passage God asked what made him hasten from his people, and he said he hastened so that God would be pleased [c2]. When he came at the appointed time and his Lord spoke to him, he asked to look at God; God said he would not see Him, but to look at the mountain [c3]. When God manifested to the mountain it crumbled and Musa fell unconscious; when he recovered he said “Glory be to You; I repent to You, and I am the first of the believers” [c4]. God said He had chosen him over the people with His messages and speech and told him to take what He gave and be grateful [c5]. He wrote for Musa in the tablets of everything, an admonition and a detailing, and told him to take them with strength and command his people to take the best of them [c6]. Another passage says God gave Musa the Book and the Criterion [c8]. God also says He will turn the arrogant away from His signs [c7].

After his anger subsided he took up the tablets; in their writing was guidance and mercy [c9]. Musa chose seventy men for the appointment, and when the quake seized them he prayed for forgiveness and mercy [c10]. God answered that His mercy encompassed all things and would be written down for those who are mindful [c11].
chapters.deep_md: The meeting is told as an appointed time with a stated length [c1], a request [c3], an event on the mountain [c4], and a reply that names what God gave: the messages, the speech and the tablets [c5][c6]. The word furqan, rendered Criterion, is a topic for scholarly review [c8]. The text gives no statement that the seventy men were chosen after the calf, and this draft claims no order [c10].
chapters.kids_md: God appointed nights for Musa to meet Him [c1]. Musa left his brother Harun to look after the people [c1]. God spoke to Musa and gave him tablets with guidance written in them [c5][c6].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): Musa asks for something and is told what he cannot have, with a sign given instead [c3][c4]. He then responds with repentance and the first words of faith [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md: Not established in the ayat: what the tablets were made of, what was written in them beyond the general description, where the appointment was, who the seventy men were, and whether the thirty and ten nights were separate stages. The ayat say only that God manifested Himself to the mountain; this draft gives no further description. Whether the quake of 7:155 and the thunderbolt of 2:55 are the same event is a question for scholars.

claims.statement_en: After God took the Children of Israel across the sea, they came upon a people devoted to idols of theirs and said “Musa, make for us a god as they have gods”; he said “You are a people who are ignorant”, and “Shall I seek for you any god other than God, when He has favoured you over the worlds?”
God told Musa “We have tried your people after you, and the Samiri has led them astray.”

Musa returned to his people angry and grieved and said “My people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise? Did the covenant seem long to you, or did you want anger from your Lord to descend on you, so you broke your promise to me?”

They said “We did not break our promise to you of our own will, but we were made to carry loads of the people's ornaments, so we threw them, and so did the Samiri cast”; he brought out for them a calf, a body that had a lowing, and they said “This is your god and the god of Musa.” (The next word, fa-nasiya, has its subject read differently by interpreters and is not translated here.)

God says that they did not see that it returned no word to them and had no power to harm or benefit them; and that people of Musa took, after he left, a calf from their ornaments, a body having a lowing, and it neither spoke to them nor guided them to a way.

Harun had said to them before “My people, you are only being tried with it; your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my order”; they said “We will not cease to be devoted to it until Musa returns to us.”

Musa asked Harun “What prevented you, when you saw them go astray, from following me? Did you disobey my order?” Harun, addressing him as son of his mother, asked not to be seized, and said he had feared that Musa would say he had caused division among the Children of Israel and had not observed his word.

In another passage, Musa returned angry and grieved, said “What an evil thing you did in my place after me! Did you hasten the command of your Lord?”, threw down the tablets and seized his brother's head, pulling him toward him; Harun said “Son of my mother, the people deemed me weak and nearly killed me, so do not let the enemies rejoice at me and do not put me with the wrongdoing people.”
Musa said “My Lord, forgive me and my brother and admit us into Your mercy; You are the most merciful of the merciful.”

Musa asked the Samiri “What is your case, Samiri?” he said “I saw what they did not see, so I took a handful from the track of the messenger and threw it, and thus my soul suggested to me.” Musa said “Go; in this life it is for you to say ‘no touching’; and you have an appointment you will not miss; look at your god to which you were devoted; we will burn it and scatter it in the sea.”
Musa said “Your God is only God, other than whom there is no god; he has encompassed all things in knowledge.”
When they regretted and saw that they had gone astray, they said “If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will surely be among the losers.”

God says those who took the calf will be struck by anger from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world, while your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful to those who did evil, then repented and believed.
In another passage, God says that He appointed nights for Musa and then they took the calf after he left, being wrongdoers; then He pardoned them after that so that they might be thankful.

Musa said to his people “My people, you have wronged yourselves by taking the calf, so repent to your Maker and kill yourselves (fa-qtulu anfusakum); that is better for you with your Maker”; and He accepted their repentance.

The passage goes on: and when We saved you from the people of Fir'awn, who afflicted you with the worst torment, killing your sons and keeping your women alive; in that was a great trial from your Lord. (The ayah does not mark who speaks.)

chapters.summary_md: After the crossing the Children of Israel asked Musa for a god like those of a people devoted to idols [c1]. The passage goes on to recall their rescue from the people of Fir'awn [c16]. While Musa was away, the Samiri brought out a calf, and they took it [c2][c4][c5]. Musa returned angry [c3][c8], questioned Harun [c7][c8], and the Samiri [c10]. The people repented [c12]; God says He pardoned them [c14].
chapters.body_md:
After the crossing the people came upon others devoted to idols and asked Musa to make them a god; he said they were ignorant and asked whether he should seek a god other than God [c1]. The passage goes on to recall the rescue from the people of Fir'awn, who afflicted them with the worst torment, killing their sons and keeping their women alive, and calls this a great trial from their Lord [c16]. While Musa was away, God told him that his people had been tried and that the Samiri had led them astray [c2]. Musa returned angry and grieved and asked whether the covenant had seemed long to them [c3]. They said they were made to carry loads of the people's ornaments, threw them, and that the Samiri cast too; he brought out a calf, a body with a lowing, and they said “This is your god and the god of Musa” [c4]. God says it returned no word and had no power to harm or benefit [c5]. Harun had said they were being tried by it and to follow him; they said they would keep to it until Musa returned [c6].

Musa asked Harun what had prevented him, and Harun asked not to be seized and spoke of his fear of causing division [c7]. Another passage records Musa throwing down the tablets and seizing his brother's head, and Harun's answer that the people deemed him weak and nearly killed him [c8]. Musa prayed for forgiveness for himself and his brother [c9]. He asked the Samiri what his case was; the Samiri said he took a handful from the track of the messenger and threw it, as his soul suggested [c10]. Musa told him that his god would be burned and scattered in the sea [c10], and said that their God is only God [c11].

The people, when they regretted, asked for mercy and forgiveness [c12]. God says those who took the calf would be struck by anger and humiliation, and that He is Forgiving to those who repent [c13]. Another passage says God pardoned them after the appointed nights [c14], and records Musa telling them to repent to their Maker and kill themselves, and that He accepted their repentance [c15].
chapters.deep_md: The calf is told in more than one passage [c4][c5][c8]. The longest sequence has God's information to Musa [c2], the people's explanation [c4], Harun's earlier warning [c6], and Musa's exchanges with Harun [c7] and the Samiri [c10]. A shorter account has Musa's reaction in physical terms and Harun's answer in different words, that the people deemed him weak [c8]. Both answers of Harun are stated in the text and are not set against one another in this draft [c7][c8]. Another places the calf after the appointed nights and records the instruction to kill yourselves [c14][c15]. The ayah that follows Musa's words recalls the rescue from Fir'awn's people and calls it a great trial [c16]; it does not say who speaks.
chapters.kids_md: The Samiri made a calf, and the people took it [c4][c5]. Harun told them it was a test and that their Lord is the Most Merciful [c6]. Musa said that their God is only God [c11]. The people were sorry and asked God for mercy [c12].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): the account shows a community being led away in a leader's absence [c4], a brother who warned them [c6], and the opening of repentance afterwards [c12][c14].
chapters.unknowns_md: Not established in the ayat: what the calf was made of beyond ‘a body having a lowing’ (the ayat say it was made of the people's ornaments), the Samiri's origin, what ‘a handful from the track of the messenger’ refers to (interpreters differ; Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: any identification of the ‘messenger’ and the ‘track’), how the repentance of 2:54 was carried out, and the number of those who took the calf. The speaker of 7:141 is not marked: it may continue Musa's words or be spoken by God, and the draft does not choose.

claims.statement_en: God says He took their covenant and raised the mountain (at-Tur) above them, and said “Take what We have given you with strength and remember what is in it, so that you may be mindful.”

Another passage says He lifted the mountain above them as if it were a canopy and they thought it was going to fall on them, and told them to take what He gave them with strength and remember what is in it.
A later ayah repeats the reminder of the covenant and the mountain, and says they said “We hear and we disobey”; and that the calf was made to sink into their hearts because of their disbelief.
A further passage says God raised the mountain above them with their covenant, and told them to enter the gate prostrating and not to transgress on the Sabbath, and took from them a solemn covenant.

chapters.summary_md: These ayat recall a covenant taken from a people with the mountain raised above them [c1][c2][c4]. They were told to take what they had been given with strength and to remember what is in it [c1][c2]. One recalls that they said “We hear and we disobey” [c3].
chapters.body_md: God says He took their covenant and raised the mountain above them, telling them to take what He had given them with strength and to remember what is in it [c1]. Another passage describes the mountain lifted above them as if it were a canopy, so that they thought it would fall on them [c2]. A later ayah repeats the reminder, adds that they said “We hear and we disobey”, and that the calf was made to sink into their hearts because of disbelief [c3]. A further passage mentions the raising of the mountain with their covenant, the command to enter the gate prostrating and not to transgress on the Sabbath, and a solemn covenant [c4].
chapters.deep_md: The ayat do not say where the covenant fits in the order of the other events in this account [c1][c2][c3][c4]. The phrase take what We have given you with strength is in more than one ayah [c1][c2]. The ayah that repeats the reminder ties the covenant to their reply and to the calf [c3]. The last passage lists the content of the covenant as the gate, prostration and the Sabbath [c4]; the ayat do not say that this gate is the gate spoken of in the chapter on provision and the wilderness [c4].
chapters.kids_md: God took a promise from the people and told them to hold on to what He gave them with strength and remember what is in it [c1][c2]. They said “We hear and we disobey” [c3].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): hearing a command is different from obeying it, and the ayah sets hearing and disobeying side by side in the people's own words [c3].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established in the ayat: when this took place in relation to the tablets or the calf, the nature of the raising of the mountain (interpreters differ on whether it is literal), and what the gate and the Sabbath refer to in 4:154.
- Who is addressed is read from the surrounding passages; these ayat say you and them and do not name the people.
- The relation between 2:63 and 2:93, a repeated reminder in the same surah, is a matter for scholars.

claims.statement_en: Musa said to his young man “I will not cease until I reach the meeting of the pair seas, or I will go on for a long time.”

When they reached the meeting of the pair, they forgot their fish, and it took its way into the sea; after they passed on, Musa asked for their meal, saying they had met with fatigue on the journey; the young man said he had forgotten the fish at the rock and only Satan made him forget to mention it; Musa said “That is what we were seeking”, and they went back retracing their steps.
They found a servant from among God's servants, to whom He had given mercy from Himself and taught knowledge from Himself.

Musa asked “May I follow you on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught of right guidance?” he said “You will never be able to be patient with me; and how can you be patient about what you have not encompassed in knowledge?”
Musa said “You will find me, if God wills, patient, and I will not disobey you in any order”; he said “If you follow me, do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you.”

When they boarded the boat he made a hole in it; Musa said “Did you make a hole in it to drown its people? You have done a grave thing.” he said “Did I not say that you would never be able to be patient with me?” Musa said “Do not hold me to account for what I forgot, and do not burden me with difficulty in my affair.”

They met a boy and he killed him; Musa said “Have you killed a pure soul, not for a soul? You have done a terrible thing.” he repeated his earlier question, and Musa said “If I ask you about anything after this, do not keep me as a companion; you have received an excuse from me.”

They came to the people of a town and asked for food, and the people refused to host them; they found in it a wall about to fall, and he set it straight; Musa said “If you wished, you could have taken a payment for it.”
He said “This is the parting between me and you; I will inform you of the interpretation of what you were not able to be patient about.”
The boat belonged to poor people working at sea; he wished to damage it because behind them was a king seizing every boat by force.

The servant said the boy's parents were believers and “we feared” that he would burden them with transgression and disbelief, so “we wished” that their Lord would give them in exchange one better than him in purity and nearer in mercy.

The wall belonged to a pair of orphan boys in the town, and beneath it was a treasure for them; their father was righteous, and your Lord wished that they reach their maturity and take out their treasure as a mercy from your Lord; “I did not do it of my own accord. That is the interpretation of what you were not able to be patient about.”

chapters.summary_md: Musa set out with his young man to the meeting of the seas [c1] and lost their fish [c2]. They found a servant given mercy and knowledge [c3]. Musa asked to follow him and was warned he would not be able to be patient [c4]. What the servant did puzzled Musa [c6][c7][c8]; the servant then gave the interpretation of each [c10][c11][c12].
chapters.body_md:
Musa told his young man he would not cease until reaching the meeting of the pair seas [c1]. They forgot the fish there, and it went into the sea; when they stopped for their meal, the young man said he had forgotten it, and Musa said that was what they were seeking, and they went back [c2]. They found a servant from among God's servants, given mercy and knowledge from God [c3]. Musa asked to follow him to be taught, and the servant said he would not be able to be patient with what he had not encompassed in knowledge [c4]. Musa said he would be patient and obedient; the servant told him not to ask about anything until he himself mentioned it [c5].

He made a hole in a boat; Musa objected and was reminded of the condition [c6]. He killed a boy; Musa objected again and said that if he asked again the servant should not keep him as a companion [c7]. In a town that had refused them hospitality, he set a wall straight, and Musa said he could have taken payment [c8]. He said it was the parting and he would give the interpretation [c9].

The boat belonged to poor people, and a king seized every boat by force [c10]. The servant said the boy's parents were believers and “we feared” he would burden them with transgression and disbelief, so “we wished” for one better in exchange [c11]. The wall belonged to a pair of orphans with a treasure beneath it, from a righteous father; their Lord wished them to reach maturity and take out the treasure, and the servant said he had not done it on his own accord [c12].
chapters.deep_md: The passage has a framing of travel and a loss [c1][c2], a request and a condition [c4][c5], incidents each answered by Musa's objection [c6][c7][c8], and explanations [c10][c11][c12]. In the explanations the speaker moves between I wished [c10], we feared and we wished [c11], and your Lord wished [c12], and ends with a statement that he did not do it of his own accord [c12].
chapters.kids_md: Musa travelled to find a servant of God who had special knowledge [c3]. He asked to follow him and learn, and the servant said Musa would not be able to be patient [c4]. The servant did things that Musa did not understand [c6][c7][c8], and at the end the servant explained each one [c10][c11][c12].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): the account is about the limits of what a person sees at one moment [c4], and it records that each act had a reason that could only be told afterwards [c10][c11][c12]. It also shows a prophet asking to learn from another [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md: Not established in the ayat: the name of the servant (Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: al-Khidr), the name of Musa's young man (Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text), the place called the meeting of the seas, the identity of the king, the town, the boy and the orphans, and the kind of fish. The ayat say Musa and do not add a father's name; reading him as the Musa of the other chapters is the common reading. Whether the servant was a prophet is not stated; the ayat say he was given mercy and knowledge from God.

claims.statement_en: God says He sent Musa with His signs: “Bring your people out from the darknesses to the light, and remind them of the days of God.”

Musa said to his people “Remember God's favour upon you when He saved you from the family of Fir'awn, who inflicted on you the worst of torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women alive; in that was a great trial from your Lord.”

God announced “If you are grateful, I will surely increase you; but if you are ungrateful, My punishment is severe”; and Musa said “If you are ungrateful, you and all those on earth, God is Free of need and Praiseworthy.”
Musa said to his people “My people, why do you harm me when you know that I am the messenger of God to you?” and when they deviated, God let their hearts deviate.

God says He bestowed favour on Musa and Harun, saved them and their people from the great distress, helped them so that they were the victors, gave them the clear Book, guided them to the straight path, left a good mention of them among later generations, and said “Peace be upon Musa and Harun”; they were among His believing servants.

God says He gave Musa nine clear signs; Musa was told to ask the Children of Israel when he came to them; Fir'awn said “I think you, Musa, are bewitched”, and Musa said “You know that none sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as clear proofs, and I think, Fir'awn, that you are doomed.”

Fir'awn wished to drive them out of the land and God drowned him and those with him together; after him God said to the Children of Israel “Dwell in the land, and when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you all together.”

chapters.summary_md: Musa was sent to bring his people from the darknesses to the light and to remind them of God's days [c1][c2]. The ayat record his words on gratitude [c3] and on being harmed by his own people [c4], and God's praise and peace upon Musa and Harun [c5]. They also recall the nine signs and the end of Fir'awn [c6][c7].
chapters.body_md:
God says He sent Musa with His signs to bring his people out from the darknesses to the light and remind them of the days of God [c1]. Musa told them to remember God's favour in saving them from the family of Fir'awn [c2]. God announced that gratitude brings increase and ingratitude a severe punishment, and Musa said that if all on earth were ungrateful, God is Free of need [c3]. Musa also asked his people why they harmed him when they knew he was the messenger of God to them; when they deviated, God let their hearts deviate [c4].

Another passage says God bestowed favour on Musa and Harun, saved them and their people, helped them, gave them the clear Book and the straight path, left a good mention of them and said “Peace be upon Musa and Harun” [c5]. Another passage says God gave Musa nine clear signs, and records Fir'awn calling him bewitched and Musa calling Fir'awn doomed [c6]. It adds that Fir'awn wished to drive them out of the land and was drowned, and the Children of Israel were told to dwell in the land [c7].
chapters.deep_md: This closing chapter gathers statements about Musa that stand outside a single scene [c1][c4][c5]. His speech to his people is a reminder of favour and a statement on gratitude [c2][c3]. Another passage presents the same messenger from both sides: what he told his people [c1][c2][c3] and what God says of him and Harun [c5]. The nine clear signs are stated without a list [c6].
chapters.kids_md: God sent Musa to teach his people to remember God and to be thankful [c1][c3]. God says that He gave Musa and Harun the Book and guided them [c5]. God says “Peace be upon Musa and Harun” [c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): the ayat state a principle in Musa's words, that gratitude brings increase [c3], and they record that a prophet can be harmed by his own people while his message stands [c4].
chapters.unknowns_md: What the Quranic text does not state about Musa, as far as the ayat in this draft go: his death, burial or age; the name of his wife and children; the fate of Harun beyond the ayat cited; the dates of any event; the number of the Children of Israel; the list of the nine signs; and the fate of the believing magicians. The cow of the Children of Israel and other accounts are not covered in this draft. The scriptures that came earlier and the later traditions of the Children of Israel are outside this phase.

uncertainties_en: The identity and name of Fir'awn are not given in the Quran; none is used here.

Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the names of the mother, sister and wife of Musa, of the father of the women of Madyan, of the servant, of Musa's young man, of the men of 5:23 and of the believing man of Fir'awn's family. None is used in the chapters.
Surah order is not chronology. The Quran tells the call, the signs, the magicians and the sea in more than one place; the chapters keep them separate and do not merge them.
The speaker of 28:19 is not marked in the text; interpreters differ.

The meanings of the phrase kill yourselves in 2:54, qiblah in 10:87, misran in 2:61, the greatest sign, the quake in 7:155 and the thunderbolt in 2:55 are read in more than one way; the draft renderings are for review.
The Musa of 18:60-82 is read as the Musa of the other ayat by common reading, but this is not stated in the ayat.

The inventory refs of this subject were widened to include 2:63, 2:93, 4:154, 7:171, 19:51-53 and 44:23-31 (an additive inventory migration; see the story drafts workflow document). The passage on the mountain raised over a people (2:63, 2:93, 4:154, 7:171) does not name Musa in its ayat; a scholar should confirm that it belongs under this subject.
Hadith to add later: reports on the staff, the Samiri, the plagues, the servant, the death of Musa and the meetings of prophets, each with its grading.

chapters.title_en: The wife of Imran and Maryam

claims.statement_en: The wife of Imran said “My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb, dedicated; so accept it from me; indeed You are the Hearing, the Knowing.”

When she gave birth she said “My Lord, I have given birth to a female,” and God knew best what she had given birth to, “and the male is not like the female; I have named her Maryam, and I seek refuge for her and her offspring in You from Satan, the accursed.”
Her Lord accepted her with good acceptance and made her grow in a good growth, and made Zakariyya her guardian.

Whenever Zakariyya entered upon her in the mihrab he found provision with her; he said “Maryam, from where is this for you?” and she said “It is from God; indeed God provides for whom He wills without account.”

God tells the listener that this is of the news of the unseen which He reveals, and that the listener was not with those who cast their pens to decide which of them would take charge of Maryam, nor with them when they disputed.

chapters.summary_md: The wife of Imran vowed the child in her womb [c1]. She gave birth to a girl and named her Maryam [c2]. God accepted Maryam, and Zakariyya became her guardian [c3]; he found provision with her [c4]. God says this is news of the unseen [c5].
chapters.body_md: The wife of Imran said she had vowed to her Lord what was in her womb, dedicated, and asked Him to accept it [c1]. When she gave birth she said she had delivered a female, that the male is not like the female, that she had named her Maryam, and that she sought refuge for her and her offspring with God from Satan, the accursed [c2]. Her Lord accepted her with good acceptance, made her grow in a good growth, and made Zakariyya her guardian [c3]. Whenever he came upon her in the mihrab he found provision with her, and she told him it was from God, who provides for whom He wills without account [c4]. God adds that this is news of the unseen, and that the listener was not with those who cast their pens over who would take charge of Maryam [c5].
chapters.deep_md: The passage makes statements about Maryam in a single sequence: her mother's vow and prayer [c1][c2], God's acceptance [c3], Zakariyya's finding of provision [c4], and the casting of pens over her care [c5]. The text does not say that these are consecutive in time, and the ayat give no length of time between them [c3][c4][c5]. Maryam's own words in this chapter are a single sentence [c4]. The words dedicated and acceptance frame the passage [c1][c3].
chapters.kids_md: The wife of Imran asked God to accept the child she carried [c1]. When her baby was born, she named her Maryam and asked God to protect her [c2]. God accepted Maryam, and Zakariyya took care of her [c3]. When he found food with her, she told him it was from God [c4].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): the chapter links a mother's prayer [c2], a guardian's care [c3] and a young woman's answer that her provision is from God [c4]. It may prompt reflection on dedication and trust [c1][c4].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established in the ayat: the name of Imran's wife, the dates, how the casting of pens was done, what kind of provision Zakariyya found, and what the mihrab was (the ayat use the word without describing a place).
- Whether this Imran is the same as the father of anyone else in the Quran is not stated. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: any identification of this Imran with the father of Musa and Harun.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the personal name of Maryam's mother, and the place of her upbringing.

claims.statement_en: The angels said “Maryam, God has chosen you and purified you and chosen you over the women of the worlds,” and “Maryam, be devout to your Lord, and prostrate and bow with those who bow.”
The angels said “Maryam, God gives you glad tidings of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam, distinguished in this world and the Hereafter and among those brought near.”
He will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity, and is of the righteous.
She said “My Lord, how can I have a child when no human has touched me?” and was told “Thus God creates what He wills; when He decrees a matter He only says to it ‘be,’ and it is.”
In another passage, she withdrew from her family to an eastern place and took a screen from them; God sent to her Our Spirit.
She said “I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are mindful of Him.” He said “I am only a messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure boy.”

She said “How can I have a boy when no human has touched me and I have not been unchaste?” He said “So it is. Your Lord says: It is easy for Me; and so that We make him a sign for the people and a mercy from Us; and it is a matter decreed.”

chapters.summary_md: The angels told Maryam that God had chosen and purified her [c1]. They gave her glad tidings of a word from Him whose name is the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam [c2], who would speak in the cradle and in maturity [c3]. She asked how she could have a child [c4][c7], and was told it is easy for God [c7]. Another passage tells it with God's Spirit sent to her [c5][c6].
chapters.body_md:
The angels said to Maryam that God had chosen her, purified her and chosen her over the women of the worlds, and told her to be devout, to prostrate and to bow with those who bow [c1]. They gave her glad tidings of a word from God whose name is the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam, distinguished in this world and the Hereafter and among those brought near [c2]. He would speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity and be of the righteous [c3]. She asked how she could have a child when no human had touched her, and was told that God creates what He wills, and when He decrees a matter He says to it be, and it is [c4].

Another passage tells that she withdrew from her family to an eastern place and took a screen from them, and God sent to her Our Spirit [c5]. She said she sought refuge in the Most Merciful if the one who came was mindful of Him; he said he was only a messenger of her Lord, to give her a pure boy [c6]. She asked how she could have a boy when no human had touched her and she had not been unchaste, and he said it was so, that it was easy for her Lord, that He would make him a sign for the people and a mercy from Him, and that it was a matter decreed [c7].
chapters.deep_md: The passages tell the announcement with a different speaker: the angels in the first [c1][c2] and Our Spirit, who calls himself a messenger of her Lord, in the other [c5][c6]. The question of the mother is the same in both and is answered in similar terms [c4][c7]. The name and titles are given in the first passage: a word from Him, the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam [c2]. The phrase a sign for the people and a mercy from Us is given in the other [c7]. The cradle speech is announced here [c3] and told in a later chapter.
chapters.kids_md: The angels told Maryam that God had chosen her [c1]. They gave her good news of a baby called Isa [c2]. Maryam asked how she could have a baby, and she was told that God creates whatever He wants [c4]. God said it is easy for Him [c7].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): the ayat show a young woman asking a sincere question and being answered directly [c4][c7]; they begin with being told to be devout [c1].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established in the ayat: the place in the east, the date, and how the screen was set.
- The ayat say Our Spirit and a messenger of your Lord. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the name of the angel (Jibril).
- The meaning of a word from Him is read in more than one way by interpreters; this draft gives the words only.
- The ayat do not describe the form in which the messenger came, and the draft does not describe it.

claims.statement_en: She conceived him and withdrew with him to a remote place.
The pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree; she said “If only I had died before this and had been something forgotten and lost.”
She was called from beneath her: “Do not grieve; your Lord has placed beneath you a sariyy.”

She was told “Shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you fresh ripe dates. So eat and drink and be comforted. If you see any human, say ‘I have vowed a fast to the Most Merciful, so I will not speak today to any human.’”
In another passage, God says that He breathed into the one who guarded her chastity of His spirit, and made her and her son a sign for the worlds.
A further passage says that God made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign, and gave them refuge on a high ground, a place of rest and of flowing water.
Maryam, daughter of Imran, guarded her chastity, and God breathed into it of His spirit; she believed in the words of her Lord and His books, and was of the devout.

chapters.summary_md: Maryam conceived and withdrew to a remote place [c1]. In labour she came to the trunk of a palm tree and said she wished she had died before this [c2]. She was called not to grieve, told of a sariyy beneath her [c3], and told to shake the palm tree, eat and drink, and say she had vowed a fast [c4]. Other passages call her and her son a sign [c5][c6][c7].
chapters.body_md:
Maryam conceived him and withdrew with him to a remote place [c1]. The pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree, and she said she wished she had died before this and been something forgotten and lost [c2]. She was called from beneath her not to grieve, because her Lord had placed beneath her a sariyy [c3]. She was told to shake the trunk of the palm tree toward her so that fresh ripe dates would fall, to eat and drink and be comforted, and if she saw any human, to say that she had vowed a fast to the Most Merciful and would not speak that day to any human [c4].

Other passages speak of the same woman [c5][c6][c7]. One says God breathed into her of His spirit and made her and her son a sign for the worlds [c5]. Another says that God made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign and gave them refuge on a high ground with rest and flowing water [c6]. A further passage names Maryam, daughter of Imran, who guarded her chastity and was breathed into of God's spirit; she believed in the words of her Lord and His books and was of the devout [c7].
chapters.deep_md: The other passages summarise the same event in one sentence each [c5][c6][c7], and all use the word sign or an equivalent for her and her son, except the last, which gives her belief and devotion [c7]. In the main account, the narrative moves from her grief [c2] to a series of instructions [c3][c4]. The ayat do not say who called her from beneath her [c3], and they do not say what the word sariyy refers to (a stream or a noble one are both discussed by interpreters) [c3]. The high ground of 23:50 is not stated to be the place of 19:22 [c1][c6].
chapters.kids_md: Maryam went to a quiet place, and when the baby was about to be born she came to a palm tree [c1][c2]. She was told not to be sad, and to shake the palm tree so that dates would fall for her to eat [c3][c4]. God says that she and her son are a sign for everyone [c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): the account records a woman in distress being given food and drink and told not to grieve [c3][c4]. The passages also record that she believed in the words of her Lord and was devout [c7].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established in the ayat: the place, the date, who called to her from beneath her (19:24), what the word sariyy means here, what the remote place and the high ground refer to, and the length of time.
- Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: the names of the places given in tradition for the birth.
- The details of her fast of silence beyond the sentence in 19:26 are not given.

claims.statement_en: She came to her people carrying him; they said “Maryam, you have done a monstrous thing. Sister of Harun, your father was not a man of evil and your mother was not unchaste.”
She pointed to him; they said “How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?”
He said “I am the servant of God; He has given me the Book and made me a prophet.”
He said “He has made me blessed wherever I am, and enjoined on me prayer and zakat as long as I live, and dutiful to my mother, and has not made me a tyrant, wretched.”
He said “Peace be upon me the day I was born, the day I die, and the day I am raised alive.”
God says “That is Isa, son of Maryam, the word of truth about which they dispute.”
God says it is not for Him to take a son, glory be to Him; when He decrees a matter He only says to it ‘be,’ and it is.
The next ayah says “Indeed, God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him; this is a straight path.” (The ayah does not mark the speaker.)
The angels had told Maryam in advance that he would speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity.

chapters.summary_md: Maryam came to her people with the child and they reproached her [c1]. She pointed to him [c2], and he said he was the servant of God who had given him the Book and made him a prophet [c3]. He spoke of prayer, zakat and dutifulness to his mother [c4] and of peace upon him on the day of his birth, his death and his being raised [c5]. God says this is the word of truth about which they dispute [c6] and that it is not for Him to take a son [c7].
chapters.body_md:
She came to her people carrying him, and they said she had done a monstrous thing and reminded her that her father was not a man of evil and her mother was not unchaste, addressing her as sister of Harun [c1]. She pointed to him, and they asked how they could speak to one in the cradle, a child [c2]. He said “I am the servant of God; He has given me the Book and made me a prophet” [c3]. He said God had made him blessed wherever he was, had enjoined on him prayer and zakat as long as he lived, made him dutiful to his mother and had not made him a tyrant, wretched [c4]. He said “Peace be upon me the day I was born, the day I die, and the day I am raised alive” [c5].

God says this is Isa, son of Maryam, the word of truth about which they dispute [c6], and that it is not for God to take a son; when He decrees a matter He only says to it be, and it is [c7]. The next ayah states that God is the Lord of both and calls to worship Him, as a straight path [c8]. The angels had already told Maryam that he would speak in the cradle and in maturity [c9].
chapters.deep_md: The cradle speech is a short list of statements about himself in the first person: his servanthood and prophethood [c3], his blessing and obligations [c4], and peace upon him at birth, at death and at being raised [c5]. The text then gives God's own words on the subject of dispute [c6][c7]. The speaker of 19:36 is not marked in the ayah [c8]; interpreters read it as the words of Isa or of God, and this draft makes no choice. The announcement that he would speak in the cradle and in maturity was made earlier to Maryam [c9].
chapters.kids_md: When Maryam brought her baby to her people, she pointed to him [c2]. The baby said “I am the servant of God; He has given me the Book and made me a prophet” [c3]. He also said that God had enjoined on him prayer and being dutiful to his mother [c4].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): the first words recorded of Isa are about being a servant of God [c3]. The chapter may be read as a reminder that his own statement of his role comes first [c3][c6].
chapters.unknowns_md:
- Not established in the ayat: the day or place of the cradle speech, who the people were, and what is meant by the Book he was given at that time.
- The sense of sister of Harun in 19:28 is read in more than one way by interpreters. Named in later tradition, not in the Quranic text: any identification of the Harun addressed there.
- The speaker of 19:36 is not marked in the text.
- The speech in maturity announced in 3:46 is not recorded in this chapter.

claims.statement_en: God will teach him the Book, the wisdom, the Torah and the Injil.
He will be a messenger to the Children of Israel, who says “I have come to you with a sign from your Lord.”

He said “I create for you from clay the likeness of a bird, then I breathe into it and it becomes a bird by God's permission; I heal the blind from birth and the leper, and I bring the dead to life by God's permission; and I inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses. In that is a sign for you, if you are believers.”
He said “I confirm what is before me of the Torah and I make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you; I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, so be mindful of God and obey me.”
He said “Indeed, God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him; this is a straight path.”

In another passage, God recalls to Isa His favour upon him and his mother: He strengthened him with the Holy Spirit so that he spoke to people in the cradle and in maturity, taught him the Book, the wisdom, the Torah and the Injil, he created from clay the likeness of a bird by God's permission and breathed into it and it became a bird by His permission, healed the blind from birth and the leper by His permission, and brought the dead out by His permission.
God says He restrained the Children of Israel from him when he came to them with clear proofs, and those of them who disbelieved said “This is nothing but clear magic.”

In another passage, when Isa came with clear proofs he said “I have come to you with wisdom, and to make clear to you some of what you differ about; so be mindful of God and obey me. Indeed, God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him; this is a straight path.”

chapters.summary_md: Isa was taught the Book, the wisdom, the Torah and the Injil [c1], and sent as a messenger to the Children of Israel [c2]. He said he made a bird-likeness from clay, healed the blind and the leper and brought the dead to life, all by God's permission [c3][c6]. He confirmed the Torah [c4] and told them to worship God, his Lord and theirs [c5][c8].
chapters.body_md:
God will teach him the Book, the wisdom, the Torah and the Injil [c1]. He will be a messenger to the Children of Israel, and say that he has come with a sign from their Lord [c2]. He said that he creates for them from clay the likeness of a bird, breathes into it and it becomes a bird by God's permission, heals the blind from birth and the leper, brings the dead to life by God's permission, and informs them of what they eat and store in their houses [c3]. He said he confirms what was before him of the Torah and makes lawful for them some of what was forbidden, and told them to be mindful of God and obey him [c4]. He said God is his Lord and theirs and told them to worship Him [c5].

In another passage, God recalls His favour on Isa and his mother: strengthening him with the Holy Spirit, teaching him, and the signs, each by His permission [c6]. He restrained the Children of Israel from him when he came with clear proofs, and those who disbelieved said it was clear magic [c7]. In another passage, Isa says he has come with wisdom and to make clear some of what they differ about, and again that God is his Lord and theirs [c8].
chapters.deep_md: The signs are listed in Isa's own words [c3] and again in God's recollection [c6], with near-identical wording. In both, each sign is qualified as being by God's permission [c3][c6]. The statement that he confirms the Torah comes with the lawful and the forbidden [c4]. The call to worship God, my Lord and your Lord, closes his speech in more than one passage [c5][c8]. The people's response is recorded as clear magic [c7].
chapters.kids_md: God taught Isa the Book and the wisdom [c1]. Isa was sent to the Children of Israel with signs from God [c2]. By God's permission he made a bird shape out of clay and it became a bird, and he healed the blind and the leper [c3]. He told his people to worship God, his Lord and their Lord [c5].
chapters.lessons_md: Educational interpretation (not scripture): every sign in the ayat is attributed ‘by God's permission’ [c3][c6], and the message that follows is to worship God [c5][c8].
chapters.unknowns_md: Not established in the ayat: where and when each sign took place, who was healed, who was brought back to life, how many signs there were, and what the Injil contained beyond the statement of 5:46. The Injil and the Torah mentioned here are named as books given or confirmed; the text of any existing scripture of those names is outside this phase.

claims.statement_en: God sent Isa son of Maryam in the footsteps of the earlier prophets, confirming the Torah before him, and gave him the Injil, in which is guidance and light, confirming the Torah before it, and guidance and admonition for the mindful.
